en: Since the accomplishment of the Blessed One Vajrasattva and other siddhis is preceded by the maṇḍala, [the author] speaks of the painted maṇḍala—which resembles the visualized maṇḍala—beginning with the words "Now," and so forth. "From this" means because without this [maṇḍala], there are no siddhis. Regarding "the great maṇḍala": it is "great" because it consists of both cause and fruit and because it possesses supramundane qualities; it is a "maṇḍala" because it is the *bodhicitta*, as was stated previously. Through the conviction (*adhimokṣa*) that it has that nature, even the *raja-maṇḍala* (dust maṇḍala) is called the "great maṇḍala. For this very reason, it is supreme.

This very point he clarifies with the words beginning "vajra" and so forth. "Vajra" is emptiness (*śūnyatā*); that which has this as its sphere (*dhātu*) or nature (*prakṛti*) is the "Vajradhātu," whose essence is the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*). Because it illuminates that [Vajradhātu] and because there is the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) of identity with it, it is "one whose form is equal to that. Alternatively, one might object: "If the Maṇḍala is the Vajra of the Mind of Awakening, then it will not consist of the six families (*ṣaṭkula*. To this he says: "Vajra" and so forth. That Maṇḍala indeed consists of the six families.

Because Vairocana and the others were made equal by Vajradhātu, that is, by Vajradhara, through being endowed with the sovereign flavor (*adhipatirasa*), such is the meaning of "in which [there are] forms. For this very reason, its name is remembered as "Vajradhātu" in detail in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* and other tantras.
% *Tattvasaṃgraha*

"Having purified" means according to the ritual procedure, such as by the formal acquisition of the ground (*bhūparigraha*) and so forth. "The Mahāmudrā is the form of the deity"—the meaning is that it is that in which there is the formal acquisition of her [form], namely, through intense meditation according to the ritual procedure, preceded by the yoga of the presiding deity. This is the Vajradhātu Maṇḍala. "The Mantrin" means reciting the mantra as appropriate, while surveying the entire site of the maṇḍala for the purpose of dispelling obstacles.

With a new [thread]—one that has not long been produced, is unused, firm, joined with the Sage (*muni*), well-twisted, and made into a thread of knowledge; with a proper measure, its length being twice the dimension of the maṇḍala; beautiful, endowed with five colors, and free from knots; and by one who is wise, knowing the ritual procedure for the maṇḍala, and skilled in works such as painting—as specified by particular measures of the hand and so forth. As it is said in the *Nāgabuddhi-Viṃśatividhi* (4.19): "Starting from one cubit up to a thousand cubits."

"By capacity" means having ascertained one's ability to procure the materials for writing and so forth. By speaking thus, he sets aside the restriction regarding the size of the mandala. "Mandala" refers to the wheel (*cakra*), according to the statement: "They call the wheel the mandala.
(Śaṃvara 9.428ab)

It is four-cornered (caturasra), meaning square, because it is without partiality due to the equality of Buddhas and non-Buddhas. The doors are one-eighth the size of the wheel. The measurement of the arches (toraṇa) is three times that of the doors. It is joined by four lines, made level by the lines of the four directions and the diagonal lines. At all four doors, in the eight joints of the projections (niryūha), this is the outer joint of the two door-projections. [The decoration is] with jewels and vajras—vajras upon jewels situated on half-moons. "Of that" refers to the outer mandala. It is circular, resembling a wheel.

Regarding the *Guhyasamājatantra* (4.10ab), because of the statement, "One should draw a circular wheel within that," and because that [inner wheel] is half the size of the outer mandala, one should again mark out the city, which is the mandala, with the vajra-line and the blue-vajra-garland line; for it is delimited by these two, since this vajra-garland is situated between the two circular lines at the edge of the inner mandala. There are eight pillars: a wheel-pillar, a jewel-pillar, a lotus-pillar, and a sword-pillar. [The phrase] "situated upon the vajra-pillars" refers to these.

The tops of the pillars are marked by vajras arranged in vajra-garlands; when those [pillars] are established, their configurations are such that, together with the inner chamber, it is adorned as if by five maṇḍalas, including the chamber of the Tathāgata and the chambers of Locanā and the others—thus making nine. However, the mention of "five" is intended to demonstrate the sovereignty of the Tathāgatas. Excluding the inner chamber, it is adorned by eight. And so it has been said in the *Maṇḍalavidhi* by Dīpaṃkarabhadra: % Q Dīpaṃkarabhadra Maṇḍalavidhi (232-233ab)
Within that is a wheel resembling eight circles,
adorned all around by half the size of the outer wheel;
it is auspicious, fashioned with wheel-pillars and the like, and encircled by a garland of vajras.

"Resembling an eight-maṇḍala" means similar to an eight-maṇḍala. Regarding "the image of the Buddha": having drawn the seats of the moon and so forth in their proper places, one should, as appropriate, write the seed-syllables, the symbols, or the hand-gestures (*hasta-mudrā*) of Vajradhara and the others. Thus it is said in the *Abhidhānottara-tantra*:
"The first is the maṇḍala of letters; the second is the maṇḍala of symbols."
The third is the hand-gesture (*hastamudrā*), the fourth is the image (*rūpaka*), the fifth is the flower-offering (*puṣpapūjā*), and the sixth is indeed the maṇḍala of the assembly (*gaṇamaṇḍala*).

As for the image, it consists of what is painted on cloth, cast, forged, or fashioned through new craftsmanship; it is the form of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) whose nature is wisdom and means, and not merely that which resides in pigment.

Because of the statement: "The consort of the Buddha was concealed for the benefit of the non-Buddhists," and because of the statement: "But in the assembly of unworthy people, she is not in her literal form. The phrase "the temple of the deity" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for a place that is pleasing to the mind. The "mantrin" is one who is endowed with the protection-mantra for the yoga of the place and the self. "By the letter A" means by that which resides in the heart. The "vajra" is that which has *hūṃ* as its seed-syllable and *hūṃ* within its core.

"By the rite" means: having removed ordinary ego-grasping through conviction in emptiness (*śūnyatādhimokṣa*), one instantly resolves oneself to be Vajrasattva, endowed with the colors, insignia, and so forth that will be described hereafter; [this occurs] by the radiation of the sixteen goddesses from the light rays of his seed-syllable. "They say"—thus says the practitioner—"May they attend!"—meaning may they look upon [me] attentively. "One named so-and-so"—having ascertained this, [he states] the two acceptances (*abhyupagata*) and the two ripenings (*paripāka*). And these two vows (*saṃvara*) constitute the conduct of engagement (*pravṛttiśīla*).

Because he has undertaken to deliver the world, he exercises the *ahaṃkāra* (the "I-sense"). "Firmly" means with an unswerving progress due to his irreversible state. "Dharma" refers to the *bodhicitta*, which consists of cause and fruit. Its "other body" (*aparakāya*) consists of the Buddha as the fruit and the Bodhisattva Saṅgha as the cause; these are the three supreme Jewels because they are the cause of unsurpassed delight and because they are difficult to find. The compound "the Three" (*traya*) is formed from the collection of these three. For this very reason it is "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*), since there is nothing superior to it.

It is called *saṃvara* because it restrains (*saṃvṛṇoti*) body, speech, and mind from obscurations (*āvṛti*). It is the production of the wholesome. Born from the application of wisdom, its intrinsic nature is Vairocana. This is because this *saṃvara* is primarily characterized by the purification of delusion. "Seal" refers to the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*). Regarding "in reality": the realities of the vajra, the bell, and the great seals will be explained in the twenty-ninth and thirtieth [chapters]. By this, the undertaking of the three pledges (*trisamaya*) has been stated.

The teacher (*ācārya*) is the guru who is the cause for the arising of the knowledge of reality; he accepts that very state as his own. And this vow (*saṃvara*) belongs to the family of Akṣobhya because of the predominance of the knowledge of reality; thus it is said: "The Great Vajra Family Accumulation" (*mahāvajrakuloccaya*). The "Great Vajra" (*mahāvajra*) is Akṣobhya. He alone is the "family" (*kula*) because from him there arises an immeasurable manifestation. For this very reason, they are "accumulated" (*uccīyante*); it is called an "accumulation" (*uccaya*) because various deities arise from it. "The fourfold giving" (*caturdāna*) is a collective compound: the four [types of] giving are the gift of Dharma, material goods, fearlessness, and pleasant speech.

Alternatively, there are gifts of wealth (*artha*), super-wealth (*atyartha*), limbs (*aṅga*), and super-limbs (*atyaṅga*). Wealth refers to gold, silver, and so forth; super-wealth refers to children, wife, and so forth; limbs refer to hands, feet, and so forth; and super-limbs refer to the head, marrow, fat, and so forth. "Having performed six times" means six times during day and night—that is, three times at night, making six occasions. "Worthy" [is said] because of his qualification for satisfying sentient beings through the gift of Ratnasaṃbhava. "At the inviolable time" means that if it were violated, the fulfillment of the accumulations would not occur.

It is "delightful" because it generates the festival of joy through generosity. The "Outer True Dharma" consists of the *Kriyātantra* and so forth. Among these, the *Kriyātantra* includes works such as the *Trisamayarāja* and the *Bhūtaḍāmara*, wherein ritual actions (*kriyā*) such as bathing and observing silence are performed, and the deity is visualized upon external supports such as painted images. The *Caryātantra* includes works such as the *Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi*. The "Secret" [Dharma] consists of the *Yogatantra* and so forth. The *Yogatantra* includes works such as the *Tattvasaṃgraha*. The *Yogottaratantra* includes works such as the *Samāja*. The *Yoganiruttaratantra* is the *Yoginītantra*, as stated in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*:
The *Yogatantra* known as the *Samāja* was taught for the sake of converting men; the *Yoginītantra* was taught for the sake of gathering women. *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*, Chapter 13.
Kriyātantra is for those of inferior capacity; Caryāyoga is for those superior to them; Yogottara is for the highest being; and Yoganiruttara is superior even to that.

In this context, by the term "Yoga Tantra," the *Tattvasaṃgraha* and so forth, as well as the *Samāja* and so forth, are indicated. For this very reason, these two are called the "Lotus of Yoga Tantra. It belongs to the three vehicles—characterized by the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Mahāyāna consisting of the Pāramitā system—because the Mahāyāna of the Mantra system is taught in the *Bāhya* and other [tantras]. This vow belongs to the family of Amitābha, because it consists of pure and irreproachable speech.

For this very reason, Great Enlightenment arises from our own *pratyavekṣaṇājñāna* (discriminating awareness). The connection is that "restraint" (*saṃvara*) is the "activity of worship" (*pūjākarma*). It is "entirely joined" because it takes the form of worship through the external and secret realities (*tattva*). In that regard, external worship consists of the five offerings. Secret worship consists of the internal appropriation of one's own semen and so forth within the meditation maṇḍala. In that same context, the union with Wisdom (*prajñāsamāpatti*) is the worship of reality (*tattvapūjā*), because it brings about the direct realization of the state of the purification of the afflictions through the sequence of bliss and so forth.
However, the unsurpassed worship of reality is the cultivation of the thought of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) itself. As it is said in the *Abhidhānottara*:
From the *Abhidhānottara* (chapter 68): Through the practice of the words of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), there is the meditation on the womb of the deity;
this great equality is the supreme worship that awakens all Buddhas.

For it is through the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) that the imitation of the form of one’s own tutelary deity (*svādhidaivata*) constitutes worship that brings about supramundane results. And this vow (*saṃvara*) belongs to the family of Amoghasiddhi, because worship has the nature of the gnosis of the performance of duties (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

One generates the mind of setting forth (*prasthānacitta*). Regarding the phrase "those who have not crossed over": the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* have not crossed over the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); Brahmā and the others are not liberated from the bondage of the two types of obscuration of delusion (*mohāvaraṇa*); and those in the hells and so forth have not found relief. [The Bodhisattva aims] to establish these sentient beings in the non-abiding nirvāṇa. Furthermore, this twofold bodhicitta mentioned here is merely that which consists of resolute conviction (*ādhimokṣika*); however, that which is authentic has been explained according to the distinctions of aspiration (*chanda*) and so forth.

In order to speak of the ultimate *bodhicitta*, he says "Now," and so forth. Those for whom Vajradhara is the foremost are Vairocana and the others, according to the sequence to be described. "Because of the arising" means [arising] from suchness (*tathatā*). Likewise, "samādhi" refers to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which is devoid of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and mental construction (*vikalpa*).
As it is said in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (1.134ab): "For it is difficult to explain that which is beyond perception—the goal and its cause."

Having thus attained realization, he utters an *udāna*—a speech arising from the festival of faith, joy, and delight regarding the realized meaning. He teaches by pointing out the lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) of all phenomena, which are of the nature of mind-only, devoid of both the grasped object and the grasping subject. All this—external objects such as blue and so forth, and internal [faculties] such as the eye and so forth—is constructed and superimposed by the mind; because there exists no other insentient grasped object separate from the mind, there is consequently nothing that could serve as its grasper.

Because it is impossible for the mind (*citta*) and its mental factors (*caittika*) to possess a dual nature; [the term] "by the mind" refers to that which investigates. "Having uttered" [is said] because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) takes the form of internal discourse (*antarjalpa*). If it is argued that "then let mind-only (*cittamātra*) be a real entity," we say no; for even that is established as being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), since it is included among all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). How are all phenomena without intrinsic nature? Because they are unarisen. Therefore, by their very nature (*prakṛti*), they are luminous (*prabhāsvara*) due to the absence of the darkness of all superimpositions (*āropa*). Why is this so?

Because the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is unproduced from the beginning; because it is unproduced at the outset, nothing whatsoever undergoes destruction after having been previously produced. Therefore, just as other phenomena—like illusions and the like—are ultimately empty of intrinsic nature due to being unproduced from the beginning, so too is the mind, for the same reasoning applies. And here, by referring to the present and by generally explaining the emptiness of both the past and the future, the three doors to liberation—the meditative absorptions of emptiness and so forth—are indeed demonstrated.

In the interval between those [two], according to the principle beginning with "in which action," one should discern one's own body, speech, and mind—which are of the nature of syllables—as being like a reflection, having emptiness as their single flavor. Bringing to mind the meaning of the mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham* ("I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness"), [one reflects]: emptiness is the absence of intrinsic nature, cause, and effect in all phenomena; the wisdom of that emptiness is "the wisdom of emptiness"; the meaning is that the mind has the single flavor of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

That very [vajra] is indivisible because its intrinsic nature is emptiness (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and because it cannot be split by opposing factors (*vipakṣa*) due to its being without beginning or end. Its intrinsic nature, which has the form described within, is itself "without intrinsic nature" (*asvabhāva*). This means that for the mind—which is naturally pure—there is an abiding in its own true form (*svarūpa-sthiti*) through the removal of adventitious obscurations, by way of its body being suchness (*tathatā*). Precisely because it is thus naturally pure, it is the self (*ātman*); I am one whose own form is that. In other words, I am of that very nature.

Thus, one resolves upon the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of this *bodhicitta* by means of the term "knowledge of emptiness" (*śūnyatājñāna*), its culmination in purity by means of the term "vajra," and its lack of increase even at the time of that culmination in purity by means of the term "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, by means of the two terms "self" (*ātman*) and "I" (*aham*), one [resolves] its natural purity within oneself. For just as the *dharmadhātu* is without beginning or end, so too is *bodhicitta*, because it has *tathatā* as its object and because its primary body is *tathatā*.

And by means of the syllable *oṃ*, which is of a single flavor with the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*, one establishes oneself in the form of body, speech, and mind. Thus, this mantra has the meaning of bodhicitta, which is inseparable from emptiness—the emptiness of the body and so forth—and from compassion.

Alternatively, by *oṃ* is meant the Body-Vajra; by "the nature of the Vajra of the Wisdom of Emptiness" is meant the Mind-Vajra; and by "I am" is meant the Speech-Vajra, because the self is merely speech due to its impermanence and non-existence. In this way, the mantra consisting of three families is expressed by these three words.

Alternatively, because meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is unproduced from the very beginning, because of the departure of conceptual construction (*ūha*), and because the terms such as "non-arising" are like an illusion, when the initial phoneme and its quality—the nasalization (*anusvāra*)—are present, the syllable *oṃ* is produced; by this, the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) is expressed. "Emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) refers to the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*). "Wisdom" (*jñāna*) refers to the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). "Vajra" refers to the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) due to the firmness of one's resolve. "Intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to the perfectly pure wisdom (*suviśuddhajñāna*), in that the intrinsic nature of phenomena is of the form of non-defilement.
"I" indicates oneself in the form of Mahāvajradhara, who consists of the five gnoses. Thus, the meaning of the mantra as consisting of the five families has been explained.
Furthermore, these three interpretations were revealed by the Blessed One himself in the tantras and have been made manifest here.

Therefore, having thus determined that in ultimate reality there is no existent thing whatsoever, but rather that it is the dharmadhātu alone—characterized by the selflessness of all phenomena, free from all extremes, and devoid of conceptual proliferation—[one should meditate].
"When neither existence nor non-existence stands before the mind,
then, due to the absence of any other alternative, it becomes tranquil, being without an object of support."
One should enter into emptiness, which has the non-apprehension of all phenomena as its nature. However, this entry into luminosity is explained with specific detail in the *Sāgaramatiparipṛcchā*.
(Q/R *Sāgaramatināgarājaparipṛcchā*)

When entering the attainment of cessation, one takes the sound of the gong as the basis and enters cessation without being bound by it; yet, by means of that very sound of the gong, one emerges from cessation. In the same way, the Bodhisattva, having made great compassion the basis for the liberation of all sentient beings, enters meditative absorptions that are profound, vast, and luminous, wherein mind, intellect, and consciousness do not function.

By virtue of that previous empowerment of great compassion for the liberation of sentient beings, he does not fall to the level of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha. Behold, Sāgaramati, the excellence of the Bodhisattvas’ preparation through skillful means: they contemplate all phenomena as empty, signless, and wishless, and they enter those meditative absorptions common to Śrāvakas and others, yet they do not fall to the level of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha.

Immediately following this, the passage beginning with "Thus, [one should visualize] oneself" and ending with "and so forth" concerns the meaning of the maṇḍala of the support along with its equipment, based on the principle that the establishment of the supported depends upon the support. Immediately after that, a single section is appropriate; however, something has been misplaced there by someone. All the sections are indeed missing their introductory markers (*anākārṣa*). Following that is the passage beginning with "Then, that very mind of one's own" and ending with "auspicious. Following that is the passage beginning with "In one's own heart" and ending with "should visualize."

Following that, the sequence begins with "Then Vajragarbha" and ends with "all the Tathāgatas. Subsequently, there is the sequence beginning with "Vairocana in the east" and so forth. The reading is not in its regular order because the phrase "the teacher who has reached the further shore of existence" is intended to exclude mere bookish scholarship. This should be understood accordingly in other instances as well. However, we shall explain according to the actual textual order; the connection, moreover, is to be understood solely by following the meaning.

Therefore, immediately after the realization of emptiness at the moment of death, he speaks of what is to be meditated upon after the celestial palace (*kūṭāgāra*), for the purpose of gathering the seed of the bodhicitta of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). "Then," and so forth. That very mind of one's own, which is inseparable from emptiness and compassion; the instrumental case in the qualification "recited according to one's inclination" (*rucijaptena*) means "by internal speech. The meaning is that while visualizing one's own mind in the form of a moon disc, one should recite the mantra internally.

The mantra beginning with *oṃ* and so forth is the conventional (*sāṃvṛta*) mantra; however, the ultimate (*pāramārthika*) practice of mantra is that which effects the penetration of the mind (*cittaprativedha*). And this penetration of the mind is precisely the direct realization of the non-dual gnosis of Mahāmudrā. For that very gnosis—because it is inseparable from emptiness and compassion—is "solid" (*ghana*); because it pervades the entire circle of directions as far as the expanse of space, it is a "maṇḍala"; and because it is of a luminous nature, being free from the stains and blemishes of all adventitious defilements such as passion, it is "greatly pure" (*mahāśuddha*).

For this very reason it is said: "Space," and "Stainless. Because its nature consists of the accumulation of all merit and gnosis (*puṇyajñānasaṃbhāra*), it takes the form of delighting the world; thus, it is free from all mental distress. Because it possesses the capacity to benefit the entire realm of sentient beings through the emanation-rays of the glorious Vajrasattva, it removes conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); for this very reason, it is supreme and most excellent.

He indicates its great purity by saying, "pure from all the stains of the afflictions. Because it is complete through its union with all forms of prosperity (*abhyudaya*), the supreme good (*naiḥśreyasa*), and the entirety of the Vaipulya teachings, it is like the full moon. Therefore, because it illuminates that [nature], even in the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), one should visualize the mind in the form of a lunar disc. How so? From the words "all" and so forth: "triangle" refers to the *dharmodayā*; because the semen arises therein, it is metaphorically designated as "triangular" through the relationship of cause and effect. Here, the semen is born of the father.

This is a metaphorical designation intended to indicate that there is no other means [to enlightenment]. This is called the "bodhicitta of noble form. However, that which possesses both profound and noble forms is indeed the non-duality of emptiness and compassion. All the qualities of a Buddha, whose nature is great bliss, are contained within the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*); they are its *ālaya*, meaning their support through identity with it. And this, when being cultivated—the white lunar disc—is visualized as semen, yet it is visualized precisely as being distinguished by those very qualities.

"Resembling crystal and the moon, white, and like immediate moonlight. "Above that" means above the moon, as if a woman were acting as a man (in the *puruṣāyita* posture). "One should generate" means that while generating [the visualization], one should recite the mantra through internal speech (*antarjalpa*). "Oṃ" and so forth is the mantra; it is to be explained as before. He states the distinction: "arisen from compassion and tenderness"—this has the nature of the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*).
And that is always accompanied by great compassion and great loving-kindness; thus it has been described in detail in the *Munimatālaṃkāra*.

*Nisumbhana* means destruction. Regarding "the moon of awakening" (*bodhicandra*): the connection is that one should generate the moon of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), born of the mother, red in color. [It is] in the form of a star; like the stars beginning with Maṅgala, it is a brilliant light, red in color. The qualities of a Buddha are accompanied by the gnosis of the equality of great bliss. The phrase "by way of reflection" (*pratibimbayogena*) is to be understood from the previous context as well. For *āli* and *kāli*, having transformed into the form of a moon, should be seen as reflected again within two moons.

In this context, the Moon consists of sixteen digits (*kalā*) due to the sixteenfold division of bliss (*ānanda*) to be described hereafter, and due to the distinctions of increase and so forth on the first lunar day (*pratipad*) and subsequent days. Thus it was said by the Blessed One:
"The letter *a* should be at the base of the big toe, and the letter *ā* likewise on the two shanks."
The letter *i* is on the pair of thighs, the letter *ī* is in the region of the secret organ;
the letter *u* is at the base of the navel, and the letter *ū* is on the excellent belly.
The letter *ṛ* is in the middle of the breasts, and likewise the letter *ṝ* is on the hands.
The letter *ḷ* is located in the region of the throat, while *ḹ* resides in the lower lip;
*e* is in the region of the cheek, and *ai* is in the eye;
*o* is at the root of the ear, and *au* is situated on the crown of the head.
"Aṃ aḥ"—the wise one should contemplate thus within the body of the Uṣṇīṣa:
"He should dwell in this way during the bright fortnight, and likewise in reverse during the dark;
for he is indeed Vajrasattva among women and among men at all times."
Thus, in this way, the sixteen vowels represent the sixteen digits (kalās).
In the *Hevajratantra*:
"The Blessed One is of the nature of semen; that bliss is known as the beloved."

Thus, by way of the division of wisdom and method, there are thirty-two. For indeed, the five [vowels] beginning with *a* are, in their respective order, the designators of space, wind, water, fire, and earth—[the consonants] of the throat, palate, lips, crown, and teeth. Among the even lunar days (*samatithi*), they have double designations; thus, the second syllable is long. However, on the eleventh day, space arises through conjunction with wind, and on the twelfth it is intensely arisen; likewise, on the thirteenth and fourteenth days, it is so through conjunction with water.

On the fifteenth day, the element of gnosis (*jñānadhātu*) is expressed by the anusvāra; at night, however, that same [element] is doubled and expressed by the visarga of the throat. Indeed, the space element (*ākāśadhātu*) itself is sometimes established as the element of gnosis because it is non-different from emptiness and compassion; yet in other instances, it is called the space element even while possessing that nature. For this very reason, the letter *a*—which indicates that the elements of wind and so forth are pervaded by the space and gnosis elements at the beginning and end—is mentioned. And thus, it was stated previously: "The letter *a* is the foremost of all phonemes."

Thus, although semen has the nature of the elements beginning with space, there is a sixteenfold division of semen through its exclusion from what is not semen; and because it is excluded from what is not pleasure, there are sixteen [aspects] of pleasure, making thirty-two. The second moon, however, is the one characterized by abundant *rajas* in women, which is the rising orb of the sun (*mārtaṇḍamaṇḍala*). For this very reason, it was previously called the sun; thereafter, it is explained by means of the secondary sexual characteristics (*vyañjana*).

For it is thus: here, according to the scripture that where there is one element, there are four—earth, water, fire, and air—there are sixteen by virtue of each being fourfold. By the statement that "the space element is bliss," there are twenty, due to its consisting of the four joys known as the space element. Through union with *rajas*, these are doubled to forty. Again, by virtue of consisting of wisdom and means in the form of emptiness and compassion, they are doubled once more to eighty.

Likewise, the consonants (*vyañjana*) that denote those [vowels] are also eighty in number, because *ka* and the others are pronounced in two ways due to their light and heavy articulation, when combined with *ḍa*, *ḍha*, *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, and *sa*. For instance, *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va* respectively denote the elements of space, wind, fire, and earth; and likewise, there are the five groups (*varga*) beginning with *ka*.

The groups (*varga*), however, consist each of five consonants and correspond respectively to earth, water, fire, air, and space; whereas *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *sa* correspond to air, fire, and earth. The letter *kṣa* is recited at the end in order to demonstrate its identity with, its emergence from, and its pervasiveness over other elements, as it arises from the fire and dust of the space element.

In order to indicate that the goal to be accomplished is the all-pervading *bodhicitta*—which is inseparable from emptiness and compassion, born from the ultimate limit of meditative cultivation, and free from obscurations—the vowel *a* and the visarga are recited at the very end. For this very reason, the vowel *a*, which indicates emptiness as characterized by compassion, is pronounced at the end of the consonants beginning with *ka*. For this same reason, in some contexts, the letter *kṣa* is established as indicating the fire of time (*kālāgni*), with the intention of burning the fuel of all obscurations in the fire of primordial wisdom.
However, in this [text], the letter *kṣa* is declared to be a *rākṣasa*, for it will be stated that it is "established in the lower regions."

Bodhicitta itself is like a *rākṣasa* because it resembles a *rākṣasa* in its devouring of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). Thus, the letters *ka, ṅa, ña, ṇa, na, ma, ha,* and *kṣa* indicate the space element (*ākāśadhātu*); *gha, jha, ḍha, dha, bha, ya,* and *śa* indicate wind (*vāyu*); *ga, ja, ḍa, da, va, ra,* and *ṣa* indicate fire (*vahni*); *kha, cha, ṭha, tha, pha, va,* and *vā* indicate water (*jala*); and *ca, ṭa, ta, pa, la,* and *la, sa* indicate earth (*bhūmi*). These forty consonants, doubled, constitute the eighty consonants.

Furthermore, these phonemes, such as *a* and the rest, are sometimes established through the metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) of the signified and the signifier; for example, "the letter *a* is the element of space" (*ākāśadhātu*), and so forth. In the conceptualization of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāvikalpa*), both the double moon and the phonemes are perceived precisely as reflected images (*pratibimba*). For this very reason it was said: "by way of reflection. The underlying intention here is to indicate that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are like reflections. In that context, the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*) is the fruition of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
The thirty-two marks are the outflow fruit; however, at that time, the maturation fruit is the knowledge of equality, and the eighty minor marks are the outflow fruit.

Including all of this within [the context], he says "this," and so forth. "The procedure for all maṇḍalas" refers to the ritual for the powder maṇḍala and the maṇḍala to be meditated upon along with its accessories. Therein, regarding those two moons: one should visualize a vajra-form marked with the syllable *hūṃ* situated within the central calyx (*varaṭa*), like the seed-syllable of the mind of the intermediate state, located between the moon and sun situated within the vajra and lotus of the parents.

The "five-needle" [arrangement] refers to the five swellings (*sphoṭa*) extending from the hands, feet, neck, and head; it is called "five-needle" on the second side because each swelling is further the cause of five other swellings. These consist of the four fingers and toes, while at the head they are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties (*kāyendriya*). For the body faculty is the primary locus of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), and it is established above, beginning from the forehead.

Because the mind of Samantabhadra is unobstructed, it radiates as Rāma and others who possess conduct that is entirely pure, being of the very nature of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). Since that [mind] is in the ultimate sense of the form of non-arising, its arising is like an illusion; this is its "firm establishment. Its "continuous maintenance" means its stabilization in an uninterrupted succession for an infinite duration by virtue of certainty. The connection is expressed as "by this" because of that cause. Regarding "oneself," since it is said that "the mind is the self," one should remain as long as space endures.
The vajra is the bodhicitta whose nature is the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). By this, the symbol characterized by the seed-syllable is designated as the wisdom of discernment.

He indicates the knowledge of the performance of duties (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*). "The conduct of awakening" (*bodhicaryā*) refers to the practice for the sake of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening of sentient beings. Therefore, the connection is: "one should cultivate the unsurpassed [awakening]. Why? Because this ground of the conduct of awakening is the sphere of that Samantabhadra-mind, and it is easy to understand. For it is clear that contemplation is indeed for the purpose of the practice of awakening; therefore, immediately after that [the ground], this [knowledge] follows. Subsequently, there is pure knowledge.

Why? Because it is "without outflows" (*anāsrava*). They are called "outflows" (*āsrava*) because they flow from the Peak of Existence down to the Avīci hell through the six wound-like sense bases, or because by means of them the continuum flows toward sense objects. These ten outflows are: attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, doubt, the view of a self-identity, the view of extremes, false view, the esteeming of views, and the esteeming of precepts and observances.

The sequence of these [afflictions] is as follows: because one does not realize the reality of an object as it exists and because one superimposes a non-existent nature upon it, first there is ignorance (*avidyā*). Following that, having heard both the correct and the false positions, there is doubt (*vicikitsā*), thinking, "Is this the truth, or is this not the truth? Then, through the practice of the false position and the superimposition of existence upon the object, there arises a distorted view, which is false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

For in this context, "wrong view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is understood as being of such a nature [as the denial of cause and effect], and not merely that which consists in the repudiation of cause and fruit. From that arises the view of a self-existent entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). This is because, through cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*), one grasps the five aggregates of clinging—which are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and characterized by decay—as having intrinsic nature; and because that view consists in the activity of the notions of "I" and "mine. From that arises the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*): "Alas, this self and the world are eternal," or "they are annihilated," with respect to the five aggregates of clinging.

Because it consists of the conceptualization of the two extremes, such as "it exists" and "it does not exist," that [view] is the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), since one returns to [the notion of] purification by grasping at an extreme. Following that is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), because one grasps as supreme that by which one believes purification is attained. Following that is attachment (*rāga*) toward one's own view, and through that view, pride (*māna*) arises. Then, there is aversion (*dveṣa*) toward anything other than that. That which is free from these outflows (*āsrava*) is the "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*), due to the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) of the state with outflows.

By this, the knowledge of the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu* has been indicated. Regarding that, he states the explanation of the knowledge of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) with the words beginning "In the moon," and so forth. "The extent of the vajra" refers to its pervading the space of one's own preference. "Oṃ tiṣṭha vajra" is the mantra for the purpose of consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*). "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra" is for the purpose of establishing that oneself is of the nature of the knowledge of discernment. "By means of the practice of emanation and reabsorption" is the explanation of the performance of duties (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna*). For it is thus:
The performance of duties consists in the world being made fully awakened by Tathāgatas who have radiated forth from the syllable *hūṃ*, and those [Tathāgatas] being reabsorbed back into that *hūṃ*.

Having thus explained the seed-syllables of the moon and the moon-like [deities], he speaks in order to explain their secret nature, beginning with the words "of all," and so forth. The connection is as follows: one should meditate upon that body of all the Buddhas—Vairocana and the others—who consist of the mirror-like wisdom and the other [wisdoms], and which is the emanation of the two moons, the seed-syllables, and the signs, being of one taste with the world. Of what nature is it? It is "without appearance" (*nirābhāsa*), meaning in reality it is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). For terms such as "appearance" and "form" are merely synonyms. It is "without abode" (*nirālaya*); because even the basis (*āśraya*) is without intrinsic nature, it is "without signs" (*nirnimitta*).

Why is it non-appearance? Because it is unborn from the perspective of ultimate reality, due to the impossibility of its arising. For this very reason, because it does not depend upon the operation of causes, it is unconditioned (*akṛtaka*). It is pure and stainless, because it is free from the conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) such as "it exists" or "it does not exist. And that purity consists of the forms of body, speech, and mind, as well as form and so forth; it is indestructible, because it is not differentiated by the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) such as impermanence. It is indivisible, because it is not differentiated by the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) such as materiality (*rūpaṇā*). It is ungraspable, for this very mind appears in the form of body and speech.

However, the body and so forth are not graspable as a name; nor is there another mind that exists as a grasper distinct from such a body and so forth, because in the absence of an object to be grasped (*grāhya*), there is no grasping of it. Thus, the body, speech, and mind—devoid of subject and object, of the single flavor of emptiness, and mutually inseparable—are called *bodhicitta*. And this very thing is the *dharmakāya* and the "without substrate" (*nirupadhi*), because it comes into existence immediately after the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) of the substrate consisting of the five obscured aggregates, through the metaphorical application of the effect to the cause.

It is born from the nature of the vajra, having arisen as the very essence of the vajra of body, speech, and mind. For although the bodhicitta is without beginning or end, its "arising" is conventionally designated even in the state of direct realization.

For this very reason, he concludes: "Thus, the unsurpassed vajra-body. And by this method of demonstrating the secret of the body, the *bodhicitta* consisting of the fruit—which is the *dharmakāya* whose nature is the example to be explained as "all the Tathāgatas"—is also manifested. Therefore, for the sake of establishing the understanding of the exemplified through the example—that the bodies, speech, and minds of all the Tathāgatas are of the nature of *bodhicitta*—he asks, beginning with "Furthermore," and so on. That *vajra* is what has been described as consisting of body, speech, and mind.

Now, even in this state of awakening in a single moment (*ekakṣaṇābhisaṃbodha*), which consists of the diamond-like path of immediate succession (*vajropamānantaryamārga*), if it is maintained that awakening depends upon the instruction of another, then why—given that the Blessed One possesses the complete accumulations of merit and gnosis—is he not established as one who possesses knowledge without a teacher (*anācārya-jñānin*)? Nor [would he be] self-arisen (*svayaṃbhūta*). [Reply: No; he is not so established. For this question of Vajragarbha is posed with the intention of referring to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

And he merely has faith in this state, but has not yet realized it directly; therefore, his question is appropriate. However, the full awakening (*abhisaṃbodhi*) immediately following the attainment of that state is indeed without a teacher. The hearing from the Tathāgata is for the purpose of witnessing the identity of its own nature. That which was described as the vajra whose essence is the three vajras—that is it.

Furthermore, specifically meditating on the body of the Buddha—which possesses the form of Vajrasattva with the arms, faces, and so forth that will be described hereafter; which is endowed with the excellence of all aspects such as the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*); and which consists of the perfectly pure wisdom of the sphere of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*) through the equality of the essential nature of all Tathāgatas—one should recite the mantra.

He summarizes: "The secret of the body. The secret of the body—which consists of the seed-syllables of Caṇḍa and Indu—is its aforementioned essential nature, because it is not within the sphere of experience of others. By this, the three gnoses are summarized. By the passage beginning with "conduct" (*caryā*), the fourth is summarized. By the passage beginning with "reality" (*tattva*), the fifth is summarized. Because it consists of the five Buddhas, Vairocana and the rest, it is the sixth, consisting of all Buddhas; and because it is supremely unsurpassed skill through the abandonment of all obscurations along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanāśeṣāvaraṇa*), it is auspicious (*śubha*).

In this very way, demonstrating the form of Vajrasattva through the fivefold manifest enlightenment (*pañcākārābhisaṃbodhi*) by means of the completion stage (*utpannakrama*), he will clarify [the subject] with the words beginning, "The two channels in the middle of the womb" (*dvau nāḍyau yonimadhye*). And this alone is here the resultant Vajradhara. However, the causal Vajradhara is the state of being of equal flavor (*samarasībhāva*) with the world, through the emanations of the two moons, the seed-syllables, and the signs.

And this very [awakening] is here the awakening in a single moment (*ekakṣaṇābhisaṃbodha*), which is like a diamond (*vajropama*). Because it is the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) for the *dharmakāya* of the stage of the Vajra-holder (*vajradharabhūmi*), the *dharmakāya* is also described as being "without substrate" (*nirupadhi*). Thus it is said in the noble *Daśabhūmika*: "For the purpose of bringing all sentient beings into the convergence of the vast domain of the Buddha according to their inclinations, and for their complete satisfaction."

For by this it is said that there is purity of cause through the accomplishment of entering the vast domain of the Buddhas, and purity of fruit through the satisfaction of sentient beings by manifesting [the Buddha] according to their inclinations, by means of both knowledge and power. This is because the stage of equipment (*saṃbhārabhūmi*) for Bodhisattvas is like the state of existence in the past, due to the commonality of being a stage of accumulation; for in this [stage], merits such as giving are accumulated, whereas in the former [stage], wholesome and unwholesome [actions] were accumulated.

The stage of the practice directed toward death is like the stage of the *adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*, because it consists of the application for the penetration of reality; immediately following that, due to the cessation of the past existence, the stage of the final moment—following the cessation of the stage of practice up to its penultimate moment—is like the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and constitutes the stage of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the *pramuditā-bhūmi*.

Then, just as for the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), immediately after the cessation of its form according to reality, the state of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the Bodhisattvas is to be understood as following immediately after the cessation of the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantaryamārga*); for these stages are still characterized by obscurations. Just as the state of birth follows the state of the womb, the state of a Buddha is established based on the perfection of the task, through the direct experience of the entire range of objects. This is because one who is born directly experiences the objects of all the sense faculties.

Then, the state of the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the emission of deities is like the state of generating a son and so forth. In that regard, there are ten states of the embryo (*garbhāvasthā*): the state of the liquid form, the state of the fleshly form, the state of the loose form, the state of the solid form, the state of the form conforming to the [previous] form, the state of the form conforming to the nature (*prakṛti*), the state of the form accompanied by karma, and the state of the fully developed form, which is threefold: the perfection of the sense faculties (*indriya*), the perfection of the secondary marks (*vyañjana*), and the perfection of height and circumference (*ārohapariṇāha*).
Through these [stages], one should discern the common characteristics with the stages beginning with the Joyous (Pramuditā).

Thus, through such resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), even in this stage of cultivation, there is first the stage of the equipment of merit (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*) by means of offerings and so forth to the Tathāgatas and others, drawn in by the rays from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart. Following that is the state of application for entering emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Then, that state—like the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) following cessation—is in some cases the state of the seed-syllable interwoven with two red *hoḥ* syllables, or the state of three syllables; in other cases, it is merely the resonance (*nāda*), because in all three ways it brings about the arising of body, speech, and mind.

Because other tantras teach that immediately after death in the *śūnyatā-samādhi*, there arises a *gandharva* in the form of a syllable (*akṣara*) and in the form of its withdrawal-nāda; and because the seed-syllables and the nāda possess various forms, since they take on the form of the deity about to arise; and because the *gandharvas* also have various forms, since they take on the forms of desired and wondrous phenomena. Therefore, immediately after the cessation of the *gandharva*'s form as it truly is, there occurs a state containing the seed and signs residing in one's own support (*svāśraya*), produced by the seed, which is like the state of being in the womb.

In some cases, there is the state of the seed-syllable without signs (*niścihnabījāvasthā*). And that, as far as possible, is the state of the Causal Vajradhara (*hetuvajradharāvasthā*), just as before. For this very reason, with reference to this [state], he will say: "The ten stages (*bhūmayaḥ*) and the months are the beings who are lords of the ten stages. And the form of the deity produced from that is the state of the Resultant Vajradhara (*phalavajradharāvasthā*), just like the state of birth (*jātāvasthā*).

And this systematic arrangement applies when there is no melting of the deity. However, when there is a melting of the sixteen-armed Mañjuvajra and others, then from the fivefold awakening (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*) beginning with the entry into emptiness until the entry of the *gandharva*, all prior states are like the state of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*). From the entry of the *gandharva* and the subsequent melting until the stage of the transformation of the seed-syllable (*bījākṣara*), the state is like that of the womb. At that time, these two stages constitute the stage of the Causal Vajradhara.

Thereafter, the form resulting from that transformation is the state of the Holder of the Fruit-Vajra, as if in the stage of birth. However, the fivefold awakening (*pañcākārābhisaṃbodhi*) occurs twice: for the purpose of understanding that great bliss exists both in the cause and in the fruit. Following this principle, one should also resolve that the cause consists of the four gnoses (*caturjñāna*), as was stated previously.

In some cases, there is a different arrangement, as in the *Piṇḍīkrama*. For there, the form of the Blessed One arises instantaneously through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) by means of entering into emptiness and so forth; it is like the state of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*). Following its gradual cessation, the form of the Lord—arising from the transformation of the sun, moon, lotus, the three syllables, the stationary and moving, the equal flavor (*samarasa*), and the seed-syllable of the bodhicitta—is like the state within the womb, up until the placement of the syllable *HŪṂ*, which is designated as the "samādhi-being" (*samādhisattva*).

Thereafter, there is the state of a maiden adorned with beauty, youth, and so forth, which is like the state of having been born. However, because of the prior entry of the unagitated [seed-syllable] that has been emitted, even though she possesses the status of a Holder of the Vajra of Fruit (*phalavajradhara*), her white form is not contradictory. For there is no rule that cause and fruit must have different forms. Thus, in the *Śrībuddhakapālatantra* and the *Śrīsaṃvara*, they are revealed as being of one and the same form.

However, when other deities are included within the [resultant] emanation, the result sometimes appears in a different form and sometimes not; for the teaching on various meditations and so forth by those whose forms consist of compassion is due to the differences in the dispositions of those to be trained (*vineya*). For this very reason, even for the Blessed One as the Holder of the Resultant Vajra (*phalavajradhara*), a rapid attainment is described in the *Piṇḍīkrama* even without the entry of a *gandharva*. This is with the underlying intention that, even while in that state, he remains in a form consisting of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) alone in the absence of suitable disciples to be trained.

However, when [the state of melting] occurs, he is raised up by Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, and Tārā, who have the nature of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), loving-kindness (*maitrī*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), and whose forms are the purities of earth, water, fire, and air. But when there is not even a moment’s rest from acting for the sake of others, then there is never any state of melting, as in the case of this Blessed One, Vajrasattva.
(From the *Piṇḍīkrama*)

In some instances, however, immediately after emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the *gandharva* in the form of syllables and so forth is not mentioned; this is because, through the sovereign influence of specific karma, for those who are born, there is an arising in another state of existence immediately following the state of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*)—like the transition of a leech—and thus the systematic arrangement follows that [intermediate state] even in meditative cultivation. At that time, however, the systematic arrangement does not follow the *gandharva* in the form of syllables and so forth.

Thus, in this very manner, the various distinctions of systematic arrangement should be inferred by the wise themselves through their extensive observations; as for how much we ourselves must say, let that suffice for now.

"Guhyavajrapadmakula" means that "guhya" (secret) refers to that which is not within the sphere of those who lack the capacity [for realization]. "Vajra" and "padma" constitute the "kula" (family) because they are the causes for the generation of the Tathāgatas and others. Regarding "in all the Tathāgatas": this refers to Vajrasattva, whose nature consists of all the Tathāgatas; she is the Great Goddess, also known by the alternative name Vajragarvādharmadhātvīśvarī. For in another tantra, Māmakī is also stated to be the *prajñā* (wisdom-consort) of Vajrasattva. By this, the empowerment of the vajra and lotus, and so forth, is indicated.

He states what must be done after the protection: "In that way," and so forth. "Having transformed oneself into Vairocana" is to be connected immediately with "by means of the mantra itself. "The syllables of the mantra above and below" refers to *hūṃ suṃ hūṃ*. "According to the rule" means [the triangle] which has been transformed from the Vajradhara residing in the ten-spoked protection wheel; for this very reason he says: "I am he"—that is, Vajradhara and Vairocana—[referring to] the world as the support, the *dharmodayā*, and the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*).

For this very reason, it was stated previously that [the mountain] is "made into Vairocana" for the sake of this connection. Within that triangle, the phrase "the maṇḍala of the sun on the universal lotus" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for the universal vajra. The syntactical connection is with the word "should produce. As for what kind of Sumeru it is, he says: "by means of the maṇḍalas of wind and fire"; the reading is in the plural because the maṇḍala of earth is also to be understood [therein]. "Above that" means above the universal lotus, the sun, and the vajra.

The mantra is the syllable *bhrūṃ*. According to the scriptural statement, "having meditated on the *bhrūṃ*-syllable as the *mālā*," the connection is that one should contemplate the palace (*kūṭāgāra*), which is produced from the wheel born of *bhrūṃ* and is the transformation of the manifested Vairocana. Of what nature is it? It is inhabited, occupied, and praised by all the Tathāgatas; for it is said in other tantras that what is praiseworthy is auspicious (*maṅgala*).

Immediately after the completion of the palace, one should reflect upon oneself in the form of the three syllables, or in the form of the seed-syllable (*bījākṣara*), which corresponds to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), situated above the mandalas of wind, water, fire, and moon.

Since the Blessed One has taught that wind possesses five colors, the water and fire mandalas here should also be understood as having those very same forms. Furthermore, because the mind mounted upon the wind is designated as a *gandharva*, the masters maintain that the two red syllables *hoḥ* here are for the purpose of indicating that the *gandharva* is enveloped by manifest passion (*rāga*). However, some teach that the three syllables are interwoven with the two syllables *hoḥ*—red with the passion of great bliss consisting of wisdom and means—which have become the parents.

This is because of the underlying intention that the Buddhas themselves abide as his parents. However, in this context, they maintain that it is the *nāda* (sound), which has the nature of the three syllables and so forth, that occupies the place of the *gandharva*.

All of this follows immediately after the *Vajrapañjara*. To explain how its accomplishment occurs, he says: "By this mantra, *HŪṂ*. The meaning is: by means of the blazing vajras born from the *HŪṂ* produced by the double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) situated upon the sun born from the letter *Ra*.

"One should contemplate the *jñānasattva* situated in the center of the moon-maṇḍala within the heart of Vajrasattva, who has awakened through the five aspects," and so forth; according to the sequence to be explained, one should meditate on the *samādhisattva* as the syllable *HŪṂ* within the moon-vajra-fist at the heart of the *jñānasattva* thus visualized. Regarding the words "one's own" (*sva*) and so forth: from the syllable *HŪṂ*, one should emanate a five-pronged vajra. He states that this very seed-syllable belongs even to Vajrasattva in his form as the *samayasattva*. Regarding the words "Vajrasattva" and so forth:

The connection is as follows: one should meditate on that very syllable *hūṃ*, encased in a vajra, with Vajrasattva situated within the vajra-fist. To the question "Of what kind?", he says: "All," and so forth. Following the consecration of the Blessed One’s vajra-lotus, he says that one should meditate on the maṇḍala consisting of bodhicitta, located within the lotus of the goddess. [He says] "one's own vidyā," and so forth. In its explanation, there is the passage beginning with "Then Vajragarbha," and so forth. He describes the location and other details of the Tathāgatas and others who have emerged, beginning with "In the east," and so forth.

Mukunda is covered with a single-faced hide; from the playing of that [instrument], they are called Mukundas. The muraja is a large drum (*bṛhatpaṭaha*), and it is played facing upwards; from the playing of that, they are called Murajas. "They should stand" means they should be stationed. Regarding the vajra-bell (*vajraghaṇṭā*), it is green in color. "All" refers to all the female gatekeepers.

He provides the detailed explanation for the flowers and other items previously mentioned, beginning with "to the Āgneyī" and so forth. Here, the learned authorities maintain that eight goddesses—Hāsya, Lāsyā, Gītā, Nṛtyā, Ādarśā, Rasā, Sparśā, and Dharmā—are to be understood as taught in other tantras. The phrase "starting from the east" and so forth is the specification of the female gatekeepers (*dvārapālī*). The expression "endowed with gatekeepers" indicates that these [goddesses] are appointed to the duty of guarding the gates.

For the purpose of protection, summoning, and so forth, by means of the cessation of all adverse factors, there are four female gatekeepers whose natures are Yamāntaka, Prajñāntaka, Padmāntaka, and Vighnāntaka. This is due to their role in protecting the maṇḍala of all Tathāgatas and in summoning the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*). "Of these" refers to them. "Cast" refers to forms made by casting copper or other metals; "carved" refers to those made of wood and the like. By the word "and so forth," embroidered or painted [images] and others are to be understood. The procedure for casting and the other methods applies to all deities.

Thus, in this practice (*sādhana*), the following are established: the place; the form of the Adhimokṣika Vajrasattva; the confession of misdeeds and so forth; emptiness; the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); the protection wheel with its retinue; the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) with its retinue; the fivefold awakening (*pañcākārābhisaṃbodhi*); the gratification of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*); the consecration of sentient beings (*sattvābhiṣeka*); the empowerment of the eyes and other faculties; the collection of the five families; the empowerment of the vajra and lotus; the emanation of the deities of the maṇḍala; the entry of the gnosis-being (*jñānasattva*), consecration, and sealing; and the offerings, praises, and tasting of nectar (*amṛtāsvāda*).

The sequence consisting of the *binduyoga*, the *sūkṣmayoga*, the recitation (*japa*), the nourishment (*āpyāyana*), and the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) and so forth, is performed "according to rule" (*vidhivat*). This entire procedure for the mandala is indicated by the statements that it has been taught in other tantras.

In that protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*), ten wrathful deities (*krodha*) are to be visualized, namely: Yamāntaka, Prajñāntaka, Padmāntaka, Vighnāntaka, Acala, Ṭakkirāja, Nīladaṇḍa, Mahābala, Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, and Sumbha. Among them, Yama is the destroyer of sentient beings. Yamāntaka, however, because his intrinsic nature is unarisen and because he consists in the destruction of all phenomena, brings about the end of Yama by defeating the Māra of Death (*mṛtyumāra*). Furthermore, since delusion (*moha*) is Yama, he is called Yamāntakṛt because he brings about its end.

The "Bringer of the End of Wisdom" brings an end to that wisdom which consists of form—that is, the wisdom consisting of mind (*cittarūpā*). And for this reason, the Māra Devaputra is defeated by him. Relying upon specific states of mind, the Māras might advance to cause harm to awakening; however, because he abides in the immovability [of reality] through the purity of suchness (*tathatā*) of all minds and of awakening, he overcomes them.

Furthermore, Padmāntakṛt is so called because he brings to an end the aggregate of emptiness (*skandha-śūnyatā*) by means of the nature of mindfulness—specifically that which arises from impure passion or common speech—and because he brings about the cessation of both the seal (*mudrā*) and meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). For this very reason, he is also capable of defeating the Māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*). Since Bodhisattvas are those whose afflictions (*kleśa*) consist of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), he is the vanquisher of the Māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*) and the destroyer of obstacles (*vighnāntakṛt*) because he removes the hindrances characterized by all impure afflictions, karma, and conceptual constructions. "Grasping" (*grahaṇa*) is the mere apprehension of an object; "attachment" (*rāgaṇa*) is the desire for it.

*Ākāra* is the formation of the object; *niścala* is the state of firmness. *Sparśa* is the state of being a cause with respect to the arising of another internal consciousness corresponding to itself; *phala* is the state of being an effect with respect to its own corresponding cause. Through the purification of these, there arise the sixfold pure productions of the mind in the form of Aṣṭakirāja and the others. And those six Lords of Wrath (*krodhendras*) exist because their capacity is obstructed by the cessation of their opposites. Thus it is said in the *Samājottara*: "Seizing and likewise passion, as well as *ākāra* and *niścala*."
The state of being cause and the state of being fruit arise from the six [factors] that produce the mind.
The group of six beginning with Ṭakkirāja is renowned as the "Lords of Wrath" (*krodhendra*).

He is called Acala because he does not waver from the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropamasamādhi*) due to his overcoming of all opposing conceptual constructions. He is Ṭakkirāja because he shines (*rājate*) by means of purified desire (*kāma*), which is Ṭakki, through the attainment of what is desired. He is Nīladaṇḍa because he punishes (*daṇḍayati*) the blue (*nīla*) evil of all sentient beings, rather than merely seizing it. He is Mahābala because he possesses great strength and power for the destruction of the mass of afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings.

The *uṣṇīṣa* is the gnosis that transcends the three realms and is inseparable from emptiness and compassion; because it has the nature of revolving like a wheel among those to be trained, he is the *Uṣṇīṣacakravartin*. He is called *Sumbharāja* because he rules over obstacles through their destruction by means of *Sumbha*.

The entry of the *jñānasattva* into the *samayasattva* refers here to the form of the deity, which is a manifestation of one's own mind, devoid of ordinary ego-grasping, and adorned with arms and so forth. In some cases, a seed-syllable (*bīja*) is mentioned, while in others, it is the seed-syllable alone. It is called "samaya" because it is a union through identity, being the direct realization of the nature of non-dual gnosis; thus, it is "gnosis" (*jñāna*) and "being" (*sattva*) within this [union], hence it is a *samayasattva*. Furthermore, it is a "being" (*sattva*) because it performs the welfare of beings (*sattvārtha*) and because it is the object of the conventional usage of the term "pure being.
Indeed, even the seed-syllable is a "being," like an embryo (*kalala*).

Now, how is it that the identity of the *samayasattva* with the *jñānasattva*—whether in some cases with all the Buddhas, in others with the Bodhisattvas, and in others with the entire world—is not contradictory? For if this were so, there would be no other mental continuum (*parasantāna*), and one would fall into the tenets of the Vedāntins. Furthermore, there would be no object for acts such as worship, the confession of sins, great compassion, or the accumulation of merit through giving and so forth.

As for the claim that in some instances the emanation [of light] is described even when the Jñānasattva, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and the world are included within a single mental continuum (*ekasantāna*), that is all the more contradictory. For the established tenet is that sentient beings possess a single stream of consciousness (*vijñānasantati*).

If it is argued: "When multiple non-conceptual cognitions (*nirvikalpajñāna*) arise simultaneously, since they exist inseparably and perform a single function, there is indeed only a single resolve (*ekādhimokṣa*) regarding the collection of atoms of form, smell, taste, and touch, just as there is a resolve for a 'jar' [regarding its constituent parts]; thus, the conventional designation of a 'single sentient being' remains valid."

It would be contradictory if one intended to assert that the identity between one's own and another's mental continuum is real; but it is not so. What then? It is based on resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika*). Even this conviction of identity belongs only to one who has practiced for some time. For a conviction of identity with the perfectly pure sentient being—which consists of the unobscured *bodhicitta*—when its activity is firm, respectful, and uninterrupted, removes the egoism of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and brings about supramundane purity. And so it is said in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*:
When the awakening in five aspects has occurred, it was immediately stated: "Oṃ, as all the Tathāgatas are, so am I.

Then the Great Bodhisattva Vajradhātu, having awakened himself as the body of the Tathāgata, prostrated to all those Tathāgatas and said this: "May all you Blessed Ones, the Tathāgatas, empower me; perform this awakening! When this had been said, all the Tathāgatas entered that Sattvavajra of the Tathāgata Vajradhātu.

Then, at that very moment, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Vajradhātu, having fully awakened to the wisdom of the equality of all Tathāgatas, entered the secret samaya of the mudrā of the wisdom of the equality of all Tathāgatas. He became the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, whose nature is the attainment of the wisdom of the equality of the Dharma of all Tathāgatas, and who has become the embodiment of the aspect of the wisdom of the natural luminosity of the equality of all things.

Here, Vajradhātu makes a request with the intention of future generations regarding the body of the Tathāgata, which consists of the five wisdoms. For this very reason, he says "of the Tathāgata. Regarding "Sattvavajra," it refers to the Samayasattva. Precisely at that moment, immediately after the entry of the Wisdom-being Vajradhara, who consists of the five Tathāgatas such as Vairocana and the others.

In the passage beginning with "sarvatathāgata," the four terms starting with *jñāna* express the four cognitions, such as the mirror-like cognition (*ādarśajñāna*), while the term "samyaksaṃbuddha" expresses the fifth. By the term "samatā," equality with all cognitions is expressed. Thus, the firm conviction of one's own identity with all Tathāgatas is for the very purpose of realizing that equality. Likewise, the conviction of oneness with the world is for the purpose of realizing the equality of the *tathatā* (suchness) which is pure by nature.

Thus, the intended meaning is that the entire universe consists of nothing but the *bodhicitta* in both its causal and resultant states. For this very reason, one should cultivate the conviction (*adhimukti*) of identity between one’s own mental continuum and the future resultant state in the form of a *jñānasattva*, by means of the equality of the *jñānasattvas* belonging to the mental continua of others; this is the traditional teaching (*āmnāya*). Therefore, in reality, there is no cultivation of identity with the mental continuum of another, nor is there any emanation from oneself [into it]; thus, there is nothing contradictory. In other cases as well, one should infer accordingly.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that the other deities, having entered into a single deity, worship the Lord with great bliss (*mahāsukha*): in that case, since those mental-form bodies (*manomayamūrti*) are non-obstructive, their "entering" consists merely in their simultaneous presence in one location while belonging to distinct continua (*saṃtāna*), but not in mutual identity (*tādātmya*). However, if they are produced from the continuum of a yogin, then mutual identity is also not contradictory. For the deities of the maṇḍala are of two kinds; in most cases, they exist as distinct continua.

As it is stated in the *Śrītattvasaṃgraha*: "In the maṇḍala for the training of the world, the deities are in some cases created by the mental continuum of a yogin, as is generally the case with the deities of the maṇḍalas of the *Śrīsamāja*, *Saṃvara*, and *Hevajra*. However, for a person of superior capacity (*adhimātrasattva*), there is no cultivation of identity with any [deity]. For such a person practices by suddenly manifesting themselves solely as the form of the perfected Vajradhara, either accompanied by the deities of the maṇḍala or together with a consort, whether with or without wisdom (*saprajña* or *niṣprajña*).

For he, practicing that very Blessed One Vajrasattva as being fixed in the essential nature of *bodhicitta*, thinks thus: "This very Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bodhicittavajra, whose form consists of the wisdom of skillful means (*prajñopāya*), assuming a conventional form through the aspects of the five Tathāgatas, the Vidyās, and so forth—whose natures are passion and the rest—engages those very disciples who are capable of entering the path in such a state, for the purpose of purifying the minds of the realm of sentient beings enveloped by afflictions, and establishes them in reality."

Thus it is established; such indeed is the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). And in this way, one should understand the lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) of all phenomena—just as in the case of Vajrasattva and others—through the instruction of the Guru. For this very reason, considering that the realization of the lack of intrinsic nature of all phenomena occurs through this sequence of meditating on Vajrasattva and the rest, the Blessed Ones have taught that the meditation on Vajrasattva and the others is effective for the attainment of Mahāmudrā.
With this very intention, in order to conform to the minds of those to be trained (*vineya*), it was stated in the *Mahāsamayatattvatantra*:

the Universal Self performs the entire drama through the assemblies of the Vajra Goddesses.

Much could be said well on this point, but I desist for fear of excessive length in the text. Consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is the washing away of the stains of all obscurations along with their latent tendencies by means of the waters of gnosis; thereafter, there is the sealing (*mudraṇa*) upon the crown of the head with the liquid of consecration according to the divisions of the families (*kula*). Likewise, that which is the meditation upon [the deity] at the head in the form of worship is "sealing. For these [deities] arise from the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of one's own lord; without that, they would not exist of themselves. Yet, this worship of theirs does not bring suffering, but rather brings complete satisfaction.

In that regard, because the aggregates of form and so forth have mind alone as their essence, they are sealed by Akṣobhya; this is for the purpose of indicating that they consist of that [mind]. Because he is manifested through the power of the *bodhicitta*, Akṣobhya is sealed by Vajradhara; and Vajradhara is sealed by Akṣobhya. This is because the cause is included within the effect, and because the cause is manifested precisely by the effect. Furthermore, because both pervade each other, there is mutual sealing between these two. And so it has been said in the *Hevajratantra*:
"Having sealed the cause with the effect, and having sealed the effect with the cause..."
Otherwise, accomplishment will not arise even in ten million eons;

thus, having visualized Vajradhara as the cause by sealing him with the fruit, Akṣobhya, and having visualized the fruit by means of the cause—furthermore, as for that which is stated here and there regarding Vajradhara’s possession of the crown of the five Tathāgatas, that too is a sealing, because he is included within them through identity with the five gnoses; it is with reference to his manifestation by means of those fruits [that this is said].

[Objection: But surely, in this way, it is only for these two that lordship over the mandala is appropriate, because they possess universal lordship. [Response: No; by virtue of diverse inclinations (*adhimukti*), even through other means, one may discern the reality of the entire mandala; thus, Vairocana and the others also possess the status of lords. As he will state: "Whichever deity enters the center of the wheel..."
His name is Abhyudayavajra, and it is said by the Buddhas that this is the maṇḍala.

As for the sealing by the Lord of the Family through the medium of his son, it is for the purpose of proclaiming his descent from that [father] in following the father; and therein the grandfather is also implicitly included. Furthermore, Akṣobhya’s status as a member of the maṇḍala should be understood as being the form of those Tathāgatas who consist of the perfectly pure cognitions, such as the mirror-like cognition (*ādarśajñāna*), since he possesses the nature of the perfectly pure mirror-like cognition and so forth. However, in the context of sealing, Akṣobhya consists solely of the perfectly pure cognition of the dharmadhātu.

Because the bodhisattva samādhis to be described—those of the bodhisattvas Mohavajra and the others, who are also known by other names such as Kṣitigarbha and so forth, and who are embraced by the Prajñās Rūpavajrā and the others—are but a single portion of the Tathāgata samādhi, they are sealed (mudraṇa) by the Tathāgatas. If that is so, then it would follow that the five [bodhisattvas] beginning with Kṣitigarbha, the [five] beginning with Rūpavajrā, and Locanā and the others are all sealed by Vairocana, since these are but a single portion of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha). This is not so.

Since each [sense-faculty] consists of the nature of the five Tathāgatas, they are the domain of the Tathāgatas; thus, because there is the sovereign power (*adhipatya*) of other Tathāgatas, there is sealing (*mudraṇa*) by others as appropriate. For instance, even though the afflictions such as delusion (*moha*) have the nature of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), they are said to consist of the nature of the five Tathāgatas. Because the eye is extremely clear, it is sealed by Vairocana; because the ear is equal to space, it is sealed by Akṣobhya.

Because the *gandhabhuk* (the one who feeds on odors) is pervaded by a delight in odors during both the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and other states, the nose is [sealed] by Ratneśa. Because attachment to taste is powerful, the tongue is [sealed] by Rāga. Because it is spread throughout all the limbs of the body, touch is [sealed] by Amogha; because it follows after all the sense faculties, the mind is [sealed] by Akṣobhya. It is stated in some places that there is a sealing of their respective objects—form and so forth—in accordance with the sense faculties, as for example by Jñānapāda in the *Mañjuvajrasādhana*. In other places, however, it is otherwise, as for example in the *Piṇḍīkrama*.

% Jñānapāda’s *Mañjuvarasādhana* = *Samantabhadrasādhana* % Because form (*rūpa*) has great delusion (*moha*) as its basis, it is sealed by Vairocana. Because of the conceit arising from sounds such as praise and the like, sound (*śabda*) is sealed by Ratnasaṃbhava. Because of attachment to saffron and other [fragrances], odor (*gandha*) is sealed by Amitābha. Because of the spreading that refreshes all parts of the body, taste (*rasa*) is sealed by Amoghasiddhi. Because of pervading all the sense faculties, touch (*sparśa*) is sealed by Akṣobhya.
