And so it is for the *dharmadhātu*. Because of its dense solidity and being the basis of great delusion, earth (*pṛthivī*) is sealed by Vairocana.

Because water acts as space (*ākāśa*) and because it is unshakeable due to its cohesion even when divided and broken apart, it is sealed by Akṣobhya. Because fire is of the nature of radiance, it is sealed by Amitābha. Because wind is pervasive, it is sealed by Amoghasiddhi. Furthermore, because Locanā and the others have the nature of delusion, passion, and so forth, they are sealed by Mohavajrā and the rest. Likewise, Yamāntaka and Acala are sealed by Vairocana because, through the enjoyment of delusion, they consist of the destruction of delusion.

Through the enjoyment of pride, because it takes the form of the exhaustion of pride, Prajñāntaka and Ṭakkirāja are associated with Ratnasambhava; through the enjoyment of passion, because it takes the form of the exhaustion of passion, Padmāntaka and Nīladaṇḍa are associated with Amitābha; through the enjoyment of envy, because it takes the form of the exhaustion of envy, Amṛtakuṇḍalī and Mahābala are associated with Amoghasiddhi; and through the enjoyment of hatred, because it takes the form of the exhaustion of hatred, Uṣṇīṣacakravartin and Sumbharāja are associated with Akṣobhya.

In the *Mañjuvajrasādhana*, however, because they are of the nature of a specific arising of mind (*cittodaya*) and because they are wrathful in form, the eight wrathful deities (*krodha*) are sealed by Akṣobhya. Nevertheless, it is accepted that Yamāntaka and Padmāntaka are as before, despite their being of the nature of a specific arising of mind. As for the statement in some places regarding the inclusion of the lords of the families (*kulādhipa*) within the bodhisattvas, that is for the purpose of demonstrating the non-difference of their essential nature.

Regarding the transgression of the colors of the lords of the families, the Blessed One himself has spoken—containing the underlying doubt as to how there can be a distinction among the holders of the resultant vajra when there is no distinction among the holders of the causal vajra:
"By intoxication the color is divided, and likewise the heart by flavor. (Samājottara / Guhyasamājatantra 18.168)

The cause is one's own [nature], while the fruit is through empowerment; due to the distinction of the support, the phenomenon is differentiated by mantra, and knowledge is also differentiated by the dharma-mudrā.

*Madah* here is a particular kind of mental exaltation. From its differentiation comes the differentiation of the colors of the seeds and so forth. *Rasa* is a specific internal state unique to each [seed]. *Hṛdayam* is the mind (*cittam*). For this very reason, the differentiation of the primary substances such as the seed and the differentiation of the heart-seeds are explained according to their respective applications. Their own causes are hatred and so forth, as appropriate. That [seal] is differentiated by consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and by sealing (*mudraṇa*). For indeed, from the differentiation of the cause comes the differentiation of the sealing.

Where the seal (*mudrā*) is distinct, it is understood that the cause (*hetu*) is likewise distinct. This should be understood to apply similarly to the distinction of colors and so forth. Even though they belong to a single family (*ekakula*), the distinction between Vajradhara and others from [deities] such as Krodha arises due to the difference in their mental states (*bhāva*) and the particularity of their enthusiasm (*utsāha*). However, even in the absence of a difference in mental state and so forth, certain Krodhas belong to the family of Hatred (*dveṣakula*) rather than having the nature of Hatred itself; this is because Akṣobhya has the nature of the Mind (*citta*), being the purified form of a specific arising of the mind.

Thus, by way of the distinction of the support (*ādhāra*), having attained a specific basis of the nature described above, although there is equality with the Causal Vajradhara, a distinction exists regarding the Resultant Vajradhara. Furthermore, that [distinction] should be understood as being stated primarily with reference to the mental nature of the resultant vajra; with reference to speech, it is stated by means of the mantra, the seed-syllable (*bījākṣara*); and "the Dharma" refers to the mantra consisting of syllables and so forth. Likewise, the Knowledge Goddess (*vidyā*) and the Body are also distinguished by that very same seed-syllable through the Dharma-seal (*dharmamudrā*); enough of this excessive elaboration.

Therefore, the sequence of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanākrama*) here is as follows: in the morning, seated comfortably on a pleasant seat in a place conducive to meditation, one should perform the protection of the site, oneself, and the yoga with *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*. Having offered the ritual cake (*bali*) preceded by the service of the pledge (*samaya*), and having beheld the entire world of suffering beings with compassion, one should—through the instantaneous resolve upon emptiness—visualize oneself as Vajrasattva endowed with wisdom, possessing the arms, colors, and other attributes to be described, within one's own heart.

Having visualized the syllable *HŪṂ*, which has the appearance of the manifestation of the *bodhicitta* situated upon the moon born from the syllable *AṂ*, with a color like a mirror—dark blue in the center and white on the outside—and emitting five-colored rays, one illuminates the entire body with its mass of light rays; then, by means of those rays emerging forth, one brings before oneself in the sky, according to the manner of fetching a lamp, the Lord Vajrasattva together with his maṇḍala deities, extending as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven and reaching down to one’s own presence, [all] from the syllable *HŪṂ*.

Immediately after the entry of the rays, one should worship with the sixteen goddesses who have emerged simultaneously. Therein, [one worships] with the external worship consisting of Vaṃśā, Vīṇā, Mukundā, Murajā, Hāsyā, Lāsyā, Gītā, Nṛtyā, Puṣpā, Dhūpā, Dīpā, Gandhā, Ādarśā, Sparśā, and Rasā; with Sparśā by offering a universal garment (*viśvavastra*); with Rasā by means of secret worship (*guhyapūjā*); and with Dharmā by means of reality-worship (*tattvapūjā*). Having entered into Vajragarvā and embraced the Blessed One, one performs the act of passion through great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

Thereafter, having prostrated, I confess my own misdeeds and shall not commit them again. I rejoice in all the merits of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, noble ones, and ordinary beings. I dedicate my own roots of virtue toward the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening of the world. Until enlightenment is reached, I go for refuge to the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma of the Perfection of Wisdom, and the Jewel of the Saṅgha of irreversible Bodhisattvas.

"Alas! May I awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; and by practicing that path, may I establish all sentient beings in great bliss—which is free from the suffering of saṃsāra, flows unceasingly as long as space endures, and is of a single flavor with suchness. Thus one should perform the confession of the limbs and so forth. Immediately after going for refuge to the Three Jewels, one should recite the meaning of the passage beginning with "I generate the supreme bodhicitta" and ending with "until [all beings] are eternally liberated," bringing it vividly to mind.

Having thus accumulated the equipment of merit, and desiring to uplift that very world—which is entangled in the net of views—for the sake of the equipment of wisdom, one should generate the ultimate bodhicitta. Since phenomena are unarisen because they lack a nature of being either one or many, or because their causes are not perceived, and since non-existence is also not established when existence is not established, one should remain non-abiding even in this [non-existence]. Thus, meditating on all phenomena as empty, signless, and wishless, one should generate it.

Then, contemplating one’s own body, speech, and mind as having the nature of *oṃ*, *āḥ*, and *hūṃ*—appearing like reflections situated one above and below the other, of a single flavor with emptiness—one dissolves the *oṃ* into the *āḥ*, the *āḥ* into the *hūṃ*, the *ū* into the letter *ha*, that into the head, the head into the half-moon, that into the bindu, and the bindu into the *nāda*. Having established it there, measuring the size of a hundred-thousandth part of the tip of a hair, and having meditated upon great compassion, one contemplates the meaning of the mantra: *Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness.*

Contemplating all phenomena and entering into emptiness, whose nature is the non-apprehension of all things, one should abandon even the conceptualization of the mere sound. Thereafter, through the sovereign power of great compassion, one should establish oneself in the form of sound as the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) within space. Upon a multicolored lotus, there is a sun disc marked with the syllable *raṃ*; upon that is a *huṃ* born from a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*). From the rays of light emanating from the *huṃ*, a blazing mass of vajras spreads forth, forming a vajra-fortress wall, a canopy, and a lattice-work of arrows, which becomes a single, seamless whole without any joints, and extends downward.

Having visualized the ground as consisting of universal vajras, one should resolve that within its center, situated in the middle of the hub of a ten-spoked wheel rotating clockwise and yellow in color—which has arisen from the transformation of the syllable *Bhrūṃ* atop a universal lotus and sun—one is oneself Vajrasattva, endowed with the colors, symbols, and so forth to be described. Then, by means of light rays from the seed-syllable in one's own heart, one should summon Akṣobhya surrounded by the ten wrathful deities; having caused him to enter through the mouth and beholding Akṣobhya together with the host of wrathful ones within the lotus of the goddess who has been melted, [one utters] "Hūṃ."

Having recited [the mantra] and emitted Akṣobhya, one should integrate him into one's own body to achieve a state of equal flavor (*samarasībhūta*). Then, through the transformation into the form of Vajrasattva, one should emit the ten wrathful deities (*krodha*) by means of the ten *HŪṂ* syllables in the form of Vajra-Hūṃkāra. As it will be said: "Having become Trailokyavijaya, one should dispel all obstacles; furthermore, having become Krodhavijaya and meditated upon oneself as three-faced and six-armed, one should emit clouds of wrathful deities."

Therein, Vajra-hūṃkāra is wrathful, blazing with a mass of flames like the fire of universal destruction; as if devouring the entire multitude of irrepressible obstacles in all worlds, he has three distorted faces—blue, yellow, and green—with the root face on the right and the other on the left, all wide open. He is fierce with protruding fangs and a lolling tongue, exceedingly terrifying. Each face has three round red eyes, arched and furrowed with knitted brows. From his mouths, he repeatedly utters the syllable *hūṃ*, filling the quarters of the sky with green light. Upon his forehead, he wears a garland of five skulls.

He has a row of fifty heads hanging from his neck with blood trickling down; he is adorned with beautiful earrings made of human bones, a necklace, a girdle, and bracelets; he wears a garment of a tiger skin that is tearing apart; he is greyed by the dust of smeared human bones; his tawny hair stands erect and curls around him like the blue serpent Ananta; he has a red Takṣaka as an ear-ornament; he wears a necklace made of the great white Mahāpadma; he has a sacred thread made of the dark-green Karkoṭaka; and he has a girdle made of the white Vāsuki.

His anklets are made of beautiful lotuses from the *kunda* flower; his bracelets are made of yellow conch-shells; his armlets are made of *kulika* snakes variegated with smoke-colored hues. He is marked with the seal of Vajrasattva, and with his two hands joined by a vajra and a vajra-bell, he is absorbed in union with his own consort through the Trailokyavijaya mudrā. Having formed two vajra-fists and placed them upon the arms, the little fingers are bound in the form of hooks (*aṅkuśa*). According to the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, the two index fingers are pointed like goads; this is called the Trailokyavijayā [mudrā].

With two vajra-fists joined at the back and the two index fingers extended, [he holds] a hook and a noose in his right hands, and a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga in his left hands. He stands in the *ālīḍha* posture, treading upon Bhairava and Kālarātri. Beneath him is a sun disk resting on a double lotus. Having thus visualized himself as Vajrahūṃkāra, one should contemplate the wrathful deities being emitted.

There, on the eastern spoke, is Yamāri, embraced by his own Vajravetālī and marked by Vairocana; he has black, white, and red faces, holds a vajra-aṅkuśa, a wheel, and a vajra in his right hands, and a noose with a threatening gesture, a bell, and a battle-axe at his heart and in his left hands.

Aparājita is embraced by his own consort Aparājitā and marked with the seal of Ratnasaṃbhava; he is in the south, with white, black, and red faces, holding a vajra-noose, a vajra, and a sword in his right hands, and a threatening gesture at the heart, a bell, and an axe in his left hands. Hayagrīva is embraced by his own consort Bhṛkuṭī and wears a crown of Amitābha; he is in the west, with red, black, and white faces, holding a chain, a lotus, and a sword in his right hands, and a bell, an axe, and a noose in his left hands.

To the north is Vighnāri, who has one natural jaṭāmukuṭa and is marked by the Amoghasiddhi seal; he has blue, white, and red faces, and holds in his right hands a vajra-bell, a double-vajra (viśvavajra), and a wheel, while in his left hands he holds a threatening gesture (tarjanī), a noose, a mace (muṣala), and an axe (paraśu). To the northeast is Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa, who is joined with his consort Viśvavajrī and is marked by the Vairocana seal; he has black, white, and red faces, and holds in his right hands a sword, a wheel, and a vajra, while in his left hands he holds a threatening gesture, an axe, and a noose.

To the southeast is Ṭakkirāja, embraced by his consort Viśvaratnī, wearing a crown of Ratnasaṃbhava; he has white and red faces and displays the Vajra-hūṃkāra mudrā with the two fists behind him, formed by the interlocking of the two little fingers like a chain; he holds a goad and a sword in his right hands, and a vajra and a noose in the other two.

With the syllable *hūṃ*, [one visualizes] Nīladaṇḍa, embraced by his own consort Viśvapadmā, wearing a crown of Amitābha, in the southwest; he has blue, white, and red faces, holds a staff, a sword, and a wheel in his right hands, and makes the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) with a noose, a lotus, and an axe in his left hands. With the syllable *hūṃ*, [one visualizes] Mahābala, united with his own consort Viśvakarmā, wearing a crown of Dundubhisvara, in the northwest; he has black, white, and red faces, holds a trident, a sword, and a wheel in his right hands, and holds a noose at his heart with the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), along with a lotus and an axe in the others.

With the syllable *hūṃ* and *bhrūṃ*, [one visualizes] Uṣṇīṣacakrin, joined with his own Gaganavajriṇī and marked by Akṣobhya; he has yellow, white, and red faces on the upper [face], and holds an uṣṇīṣa on his head with both hands, a wheel and a lotus in his right hands, and a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) and a sword in his left hands. With the syllable *hūṃ*, [one visualizes] Sumbha, who has entered into union with his own Dharaṇīndharā and is marked by Akṣobhya; he has black, white, and red faces, and holds a vajra, a wheel, and a jewel in his right hands, while in his left hands he holds a heart, a noose with a threatening gesture, a lotus, and a sword.

And all these [deities] are to be meditated upon as standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon double lotuses and sun-discs situated atop their respective principal deities; they have the same color as the primary face, while their faces—proceeding from right to left—are extremely wrathful, red, round, with three eyes, blazing, roaring, and most terrifying.

Uṣṇīṣacakrin, Acala, and Sumbha wear jeweled crowns and are adorned with various ornaments; they are graceful. The others have brown hair and beards standing erect, are adorned with various *nāga* ornaments, and carry five skulls upon their heads. They bear the five seals (*mudrā*) beginning with the wheel (*cakramudrā*), wear garlands of severed heads hanging from their necks, and are stout and pot-bellied. All of them, together with their seats, are motionless.
One should visualize the wheel as being like something unmoving due to its extreme rapid rotation, surrounded by a dense mass of many flickering flames.

Then Vajra-hūṃkāra, by snapping the thumb and forefinger of his left hand with the Trailokyavijaya mudrā, emanates from Yamāntaka, Prajñāntaka, Padmāntaka, and Vighnāntaka a second form of each in their respective places. These forms arrive before him and, seeking instructions as to what they should do, [the central deity issues commands] with the four mantras: *oṃ vajrāṅkuśākarṣaya hūṃ*, *oṃ vajrapāśa bandha hūṃ*, *oṃ vajrakāli tarjaya hūṃ*, and *oṃ vajramuṣṭi gṛhṇa hūṃ*.

He should command them. Having gone to the ten directions, they draw forth the lords of obstacles with a hook, bind them by the throat with a noose, threaten them, seize them with their fists, and hand them over to the ten wrathful deities.

And the wrathful deities, with their left hands holding at the navel and below a kīla in the form of a single-pronged vajra upon which their own forms are established, having caused the obstructors to enter the wells near the tips of the spokes in their respective directions—produced by the long-sounding utterance of the syllable *HŪṂ*—they nail them to the crowns of their heads while reciting *OṂ VAJRAKĪLA KĪLAYA HŪṂ*, and they strike them with flaming vajra-hammers held in their right hands while chanting *OṂ VAJRAMUDGARA ĀKOṬAYA HŪṂ*. One should thus visualize [the process] through these two actions of striking and nailing.

One should contemplate the multitude of obstacles as being of the single nature of suchness through great bliss (*mahāsukha*), and the remaining obstacles as fleeing far away. Thus, having resolved that the entire world—above, below, and across, as far as the Great Cakravāḍa mountains—is free from obstacles, one visualizes within the center of the hub of the wheel, beneath oneself, upon a blue wind-maṇḍala arising from the syllable *yaṃ* and shaped like a bow, a red triangular fire-maṇḍala produced from the syllable *raṃ*, emitting seven tongues of flame.

Above that, one should visualize a circular white water-mandala marked with the sign of a conch (vaṃbha), adorned with jewels and resting upon a square earth-mandala of lovely gold marked with a vajra; above that, having meditated on Mount Sumeru, which is transformed from the syllables *hūṃ-suṃ-hūṃ*, one should contemplate the Dharmodaya—white, triangular, having the nature of the inner sky, subtle at the bottom and broad at the top, adorned at its base with a double-vajra upon a multi-petaled lotus rising from the corner. This Dharmodaya is the transformation of Vajradhara, who has instantaneously undergone a change of form from the syllable *vajra-hūṃ* and is endowed with the symbols to be described hereafter.

One should meditate upon the celestial mansion (*kūṭāgāra*) of Viśvavajra: its altar is blue, and each of the three directions has a color identical to that of Vairocana and the other [Buddhas]. In its center, one should visualize a square, four-doored, and four-arched palace, adorned with various beauties such as necklaces and half-necklaces, produced from an eight-spoked wheel empowered by the syllable *Bhrūṃ*, which is the transformation of Vairocana. This palace rests upon moon and sun seats situated on a lotus with multicolored petals and is endowed with thirty-seven [deities].

Then, having resolved that the future Buddhas, who pervade the infinite expanse of space, consist of the nature of wisdom and skillful means and possess the form of consonants augmented by twice the vowels *svara*, *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, *ḍa*, *ḍha*, and *dha*, one should resolve that they have entered into one's own self—which abides within the interior of the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*)—in the form of sound, being non-different from one's own mind. Then, having visualized them as having emanated forth and appearing on the central seat in the form of two rows of vowels, one should meditate upon the white moon disc transformed from those [vowels], reflecting the image of their very form. Oṃ.

One should perform the internal recitation with the mantra, "I shall effect the penetration of the mind. Having visualized it in the form of two rows of syllables, one should behold the red moon transformed from them, reflecting their shape. Then, one should empower it with the mantra: "Oṃ, I generate the mind of awakening (bodhicitta)."

In the midst of that, from the previously established intermediate state (*antarābhava*), through the sequence of the drop (*bindu*), the moon above, and the *hūṃ* at its head, one visualizes the *hūṃ* situated upon the hub of a vajra produced from the seed-syllable *hūṃ*. Having uttered "Oṃ, I am of vajra-nature," and having performed the integration of the Tathāgatas—who have been made fully awakened by the radiation of the *hūṃ* syllables—into the world, one performs the fulfillment of duties. Then, when the Tathāgatas stationed in the sky, who have been impelled by rays of light and have assumed the form of Vajradhara, are integrated into the *hūṃ* syllable, [one recites]: "Oṃ Mahāsukha Vajrasattva."

Immediately after the exhortation with the mantra *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ suratas tvam* recited internally, one should meditate on Vajradhara as the essence of the three beings through the transformation of all things into a state of equal flavor (*samarasībhūta*), and recite with a smile: *oṃ yathā sarvatathāgatās tathāham*. [He is] white in color, slightly tinged with red; his black matted locks are bound with a jewel and a universal vajra, beneath which is a crescent moon; and upon his forehead is a Buddha-crown.

Adorned with a five-pronged *karoṭaka* crown, bracelets, earrings, a necklace, armlets, a girdle, and ashes; having three faces—the right and left faces being blue and red respectively—with three eyes on each face; possessing six arms, his two principal hands adorned with a vajra and a vajra-bell embrace his own consort (*svābhaprajñā*), generating a mass of bliss from the union of their lotuses; holding a sword and a goad in his two right hands, and a skull-cup and a noose in his two left; encircled by a solar halo; performing the *tāṇḍava* dance upon a moon disc atop a double-lotus and a skull-cup in the *ardhaparyaṅka* posture.

With the nine dramatic sentiments (*navanāṭyarasa*), within his heart, upon a moon on a universal lotus, is the Knowledge Being (*jñānasattva*), red and white, radiant with moonlight, seated upon a sattva-couch, wearing a crown of five Buddhas or a jewel crown, adorned with jewel ornaments, and embracing his own consort (*svābhaprajñā*) with his two hands holding a vajra and a vajra-bell; in her heart, however, upon a moon, is the Samādhi Being (*samādhisattva*) in the form of a black syllable *HŪṂ*. Then, having purified the Buddha-field, one attains perfect awakening.

For the sake of purifying the realm of sentient beings, when the host of Victors is exhorted by the sound of the *surata*, they are included within the Vajra-holder; and when the Wisdom-consorts are satisfied, these [deities] emerge in the forms of Locanā and the other goddesses, each according to her own family. Upon their inclusion within the Wisdom-consort, one contemplates the satisfaction of the Means (Upāya). Then, having drawn in the Tathāgatas with rays of light from the Samādhi-sattva, and having caused them to enter through the mouth, they are included within one’s own body. Preceded by the experience of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), they take the form of the fluid of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) within the lotus of the Wisdom-consort.

Having emitted that [emanation], one should behold the mandala presided over by Akṣobhya. One should then contemplate the sentient beings here who have been mentally introduced, likewise brought forth, entered, and internalized by the fluid of the bodhicitta—which consists of all the Tathāgatas—established within the vajra-jewel. Through consecration, they become liquefied as bodhicitta and attain the bliss and mental well-being of all the Tathāgatas. Then, through the transformation of their respective seed-syllables and the purification of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, they are perfected in the forms of deities such as Akṣobhya and Vairocana.

Having resolved with the intention of attaining the state of a future Tathāgata, one should mentally dismiss [the deities] into their respective world-systems; nor should one contemplate the maṇḍala-circle.

Following that, according to the sequence to be described beginning with "the eye is called Mohavajra," one should visualize: in the lotus-moon at the two eyes, Mohavajra, born from the syllable Oṃ, white in color and embraced by Rūpavajrā; in the lotus-sun at the two ears, Dveṣavajra, black in color and born from the syllable Hūṃ, embraced by Śabdavajrā; and in the nostrils, upon a lotus-sun, Mātsaryavajra, born from the transformation of the syllable Trāṃ, yellow in color and joined with Gandhavajrā.

At the root of the tongue, upon a lotus and sun disk, is the red Rāgavajra, transformed from the syllable *Āḥ*, in union with Rasavajrā. On the forehead, upon a lotus and sun disk, is the green Īrṣyāvajra, transformed from the sword and the syllable *Hāṃ*, in union with Sparśavajrā. At the heart, upon a vajra and sun disk, is the white Aiśvaryavajra, born from the vajra and the syllable *Hūṃ*, in union with Dharmadhātuvajrā.

These, beginning with Mohavajra, whose nature is the purification of the internal sense-bases, are the bestowers of the divine eye and so forth; they are, respectively, Kṣitigarbha, Vajrapāṇi, Khagarbha, Lokeśvara, Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, and Samantabhadra—bearing the other names [of the Buddhas]—and are sealed by Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnasaṃbhava, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi, and Vajrasattva. They wear matted hair in a crown, have three eyes, five mudrās, two arms, and one face, and with their right hand...

They hold a wheel, a vajra, a jewel, a red lotus, a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*), and a white vajra in their right hands, while holding a vajra-bell in their left; they stand in the *ālīḍha* posture. Their consorts (*prajñā*), however, are the purities of the external sense-bases (*bāhyāyatana*) arising from the seed-syllables Jaḥ, Hūṃ, Baṃ, Hoḥ, Khaṃ, and Raṃ; they are identical in form to [their respective] lords, yet they stand in the *pratyālīḍha* posture. With their right hands, they hold a mirror, a lute, perfume, a conch, a vessel of nectar, a double-vajra, and the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), while holding a vajra-bell with their left; Śabdavajrā, moreover, holds a lute even with her left hand, and she wears a crown of Ratnasaṃbhava.

Upon the moon-disks of the lotuses at the navel, heart, throat, and head are Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, and Tārā; on the moon-disk of the secret lotus is Padmajvālinī, smoke-colored, with three faces—white, red, and black on the right and left respectively—and her three right arms adorned with a hook, a Brahma-head, and a flaying-knife.

These five goddesses hold a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga, and a noose in their two left hands; they have three eyes, wear the five seals (*pañcamudrā*), have disheveled hair, are naked, and stand in the *ālīḍha* posture. These five goddesses are embraced and sealed respectively by Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi, and Ratnasaṃbhava—their own pure forms representing the purification of the elements of earth, water, fire, air, and space—and by those whose nature is the purification of the aggregates of form, consciousness, perception, mental formations, and feeling. However, according to the statement that "Padmajvālinī is like Māmakī," she is sealed by Akṣobhya.

In the suchness (*tathatā*) of the aggregates (*skandha*) beginning with form, Vajrasattva is embraced by Vajrajvālinī upon a lotus-moon at the crown of the head; she is the nature of the purification of the gnosis element (*jñānadhātu*). At the head, throat, and heart, Vairocana, Amitābha, and Akṣobhya, together with their consorts, are the nature of the purification of body, speech, and mind. These deities, Kṣitigarbha and the others, having melted through the great bliss of union (*saṃpuṭamahāsukha*), dissolve internally within the sense bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), aggregates (*skandha*), and the body.

Thereafter, the armor (*kavaca*) should be visualized with the mantras to be recited: *ta*, *da*, *na*, *ha*, *hi*, *hu*, *he*, *ho*, *ham*. In the heart is Vajrasattva, produced from *oṃ haḥ*; in the head is Vairocana, produced from *namaḥ ji*; at the crown of the head is Padmanarteśvara, produced from *svāhā hu*; on the two shoulders is Akṣobhya, produced from *vauṣaṭ ni*; in the two eyes is Vajrasūrya, born from *hūṃ hūṃ ho*; and in all limbs is Paramāśva, born from *phaṭ haṃ*.

These six, in their respective order, are embraced by Vajravārāhī, Yamīnī, Mohinī, Sañcālinī, Saṃtrāsinī, Caṇḍikā, and Kroḍī. Among them, Vajravārāhī is red; her right and left faces are blue and green respectively; her three left hands hold a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga, and a noose; and her three right arms bear a hook, a Brahma-head, and a flaying-knife.

Yāminī and the others are blue, white, yellow, green, and smoky in color; they have disheveled hair, are naked, possess one face, three eyes, and four arms. Holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga with their two left hands, and a hand-drum and a flaying-knife with their two right hands, they wear the five mudrās and stand in the ālīḍha posture. Among them, the deities who are white have the luster of the moon and are seated upon moon-maṇḍalas; the others, however, have the luster of the sun and are seated upon sun-maṇḍalas.

Having thus reflected within oneself, one should instantly contemplate all of this—the form of the purification of the eyes and so forth—within one's own wisdom (*prajñā*). As for the armor (*kavaca*), it is performed in that [wisdom] with the mantras to be mentioned later: *oṃ haṃ ho hrīḥ svāhā*. Therein, at the navel is Vārāhī, born from *oṃ vaṃ*; at the heart is Yāminī, born from *hāṃ yoṃ*; at the throat is Mohinī, produced from *hoṃ māṃ*; at the head is Saṃcālinī, born from *hreṃ hrīṃ*; at the crest-lock (*śikhā*) is Saṃtrāsinī, produced from *svā huṃ*;
and on all limbs is Caṇḍikā, born from *hā phaṭ*. These six have their husbands' necks held fast.

Again, having visualized within the head of Prajñā the syllable Oṃ situated on the moon—the nature of the Body Family—dissolved and composed of its subtle atoms extending as far as the heart; then, from the Mind-Vajra, below that at the heart, the syllable Hūṃ situated on the sun—the nature of the Mind Family—previously [visualized], which likewise pervades as far as the navel; and below the navel, the syllable Svā situated on the sun—the nature of the Jewel Family—as before, pervading as far as the hips; and above the secret place, on the sun, the red syllable Āḥ.

Having visualized, as before, the nature of the Passion Family (rāgakula) pervading the waist, and having visualized the two thighs as the suns with the green syllable *hā* as before, extending down to the feet; and having made her the one who gathers the five families (*pañcakulakalāpinī*), one should observe one’s own vajra empowered by the *oṃ* born from the jewel of the vajra through the syllable *hūṃ*, and her lotus with its filaments empowered by the *bhruṃ* born from the transformation of *hrīḥ*. Then, through the stimulation by the rays of light from one’s own heart, they become of one mind, characterized by a slight smile, embracing, nakedness, disheveled hair, and horripilation.

According to another view, one who has mastered the vidyā—characterized by longing, recollection, mental agitation, and insanity, and having reached its five stages—which is the very nature of the *prajñāpāramitā*, should himself become the means and enter into union with the intent of pleasing all the Tathāgatas, thinking: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the Vajra that pleases all the Tathāgatas."

In this context, at the time of impassioned union (*anurāgaṇa*), because the meditative absorption of equanimity (*samatā-samādhi*) has become manifest, there occurs an attainment that negates the duality between the expanded vidyā and one’s own self; and by means of the intention to impassion all Tathāgatas, it negates the distinction among all Tathāgatas. Thus, it consists of the gnosis of equality (*samatājñāna*).

And thus, in the form of Mahāvajradhara, who is the essence of all Tathāgatas in male form, one enjoys and satisfies the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) and others who are the essence of all women. Then, impelled by the rays from the [central] jewel, the Tathāgatas arrive, enter through the mouth, and having dissolved, they fall into the interior of the lotus. One should contemplate that fivefold wisdom-nectar being taken up by the play of the tip of the tongue; this is the first meditative absorption (samādhi) called "The Initial Yoga."

Then, having drawn in all the Tathāgatas with rays of light from one's own heart and caused them to enter through the door of Vairocana, one should visualize them as the essence of the fluid of bodhicitta produced within the interior of a lotus by those experiencing great bliss arising from great passion. From that [fluid] arise: HŪṂ VUṂ ĀṂ HRĪḤ KHAṂ BHRŪṂ HŪṂ HRĪḤ TĀṂ; AṂ ĀṂ IṂ ĪṂ UṂ ŪṂ AṂ AḤ.

With the seed-syllables *ṛṃ haṃ āṃ ṝṃ laṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ gaṃ dhaṃ ḹṃ naṃ raṃ uṃ ūṃ eṃ aiṃ jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ*, one should behold the maṇḍala consisting of thirty-seven deities, which is suddenly manifested as the nature of great bliss, whose single flavor is emptiness, and which has Akṣobhya as its presiding lord. Then, having exhorted and emanated [the deities] with the mantras of emission, and having accomplished the welfare of the world through infinite emanations for each according to their respective families, one should establish them in their proper places.

Therein, with the syllable *hūṃ*, one should internalize Akṣobhya—black, with faces, arms, and emblems as in Vajrasattva—within oneself. Even when he is thus internalized, Vajradhara remains white. With the syllable *vuṃ*, one should visualize Vairocana in front, white and gentle, four-armed, holding a wheel and a bell in his two right hands, and a skull-cup and a noose in his two left hands.

With the syllable *Āṃ*, one should visualize Ratneśa in the south, yellow in color, with four arms; he holds a jewel and a goad in his two right hands, and a skull-cup and a noose in his two left hands. With the syllable *Hrīḥ*, one should visualize Amitābha in the west, red in color, with four arms; he bears an arrow and a lotus in his two right hands, and a bow and a noose in his two left hands. With the syllable *Khaṃ*, one should visualize Amoghasiddhi in the north, green in color, holding a vajra-goad in his two right hands and a bell and a skull-cup in his two left hands.

*Bhrūṃ*: Locanā is in the northeast, white, with eight arms; she holds a wheel, a vajra, a sword, and an arrow in her right hands, and a skull-cup, a bell, a noose, and a bow in her others. *Hūṃ*: Māmakī is in the southeast, blue, with twelve arms; she holds an arrow, a sword, a vajra, a wheel, a jewel, and a lotus in her right hands, and a bow, a hook, a bell, a noose, a skull-cup, and a khaṭvāṅga in her left hands.

With the syllable *hrīḥ*, one should emanate Pāṇḍarā in the southwest corner, red in color, with eight arms; she holds an arrow, a lotus, a sword, and a vajra in her right hands, and a bow, a skull-cup, a noose, and a bell in her left hands. With the syllable *tāṃ*, one should emanate Tāriṇī in the northwest corner, green in color, with eight arms; she holds a red lotus, a sword, a goad, and an arrow in her right hands, and a wheel, a noose, a skull-cup, and a bow in her other [left] hands. In this same manner, the other deities should also be emanated by means of their respective seed-syllables of origin.

There, in the second enclosure, in the eastern direction, is Vajraraudrī, white, with four arms; in her two right hands she holds an arrow and a goad, and in the other two a bow and a skull-cup filled with semen. To the south is Vajrabimbā, yellow, with four arms; she holds a vajra and a trident in her right hands, and her left hands are adorned with a noose and a skull-cup filled with blood.

In the west is Rāgavajrā, also known as Vajrarāgā, who is red in color, four-armed, holding a sword and a vajra in her right hands, and a skull-cup filled with water and a bell in her left hands. In the north is Vajrasaumyā, who is green, four-armed, holding a pestle and three banners in her right hands, and a vajra-khaṭvāṅga and a skull-cup in her left hands. In the northeast is Vajrayakṣī, who is white and yellow, four-handed, holding a staff and a blue lotus in her right hands, and a skull-cup and a ḍamaru drum in her left hands.

In the southeast is Vajraḍākinī, yellowish-red, with four sprout-like hands; her right hands hold a lotus and a mirror, and her left hands carry a skull-cup filled with fat and a battle-axe. In the southwest is Śabdavajrā, reddish-blue, with four arms; her right hands hold a spear and a conch, and her left hands hold a wheel and a skull-cup filled with blood.

In the northwest is Pṛthvīvajrā, greenish-white, with four arms; her right hands hold a vase and a vajra, and her left hands hold a lamp and a bell attached to a skull-cup covered with human skin and filled with the ten substances of nectar.

In the third enclosure, in the eastern direction, is Hāsyā, red in color, with two hands performing the gesture of laughter while holding a vajra and a vajra-bell. In the southern direction is Lāsyā, blue in color, with a pair of arms holding a vajra and a vajra-bell and performing the proud dance-gesture (*lāsyābhinaya*). Regarding this, it is said: "Singing the *hūṃ*-song, having first performed the dance and bound two vajra-fists at the waist, she stands to the right; gracefully, with the left side of her head slightly bent, she is Vajralāsyā."

In the west is Gītā, yellow in color, slightly swaying her body with amorous passion (*śṛṅgāra*), holding two cymbals (*kaṃsikā*) in her two hands. In the north is Nṛtyā, green in color, busy with dance through gestures such as the lotus (*kamala-abhinaya*), holding a three-pronged vajra and a vajra-bell in her two hands. And it is said: "The whirling of both hands, rotated around both sides from the festive joy of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), with the single head [of the deity] fixed in the dance—this is the yoga of dance; thus she is called 'Nṛtyā'. In the northeast is Vaṃśā, red in color.

In the southeast is Vīṇā, yellow in color, slightly moving her body with amorous grace; in the southwest is Mukundā, white; in the northwest is Murajā, smoke-colored. These four have both hands intent upon playing their respective musical instruments.

Then, on the outer band: in the southeast is Puṣpā, white in color, holding a flower garland and a wheel in her left and right hands respectively; performing a dance, she places her vajra-añjali at her head and brings it down to her heart in the gesture of offering flowers. In the southwest is Dhūpā, smoke-colored, holding an incense burner and a jewel in her left and right hands respectively. In the northwest is Dīpā, golden-colored, holding a lamp-stick and a lotus in her right and left hands respectively.

In the northeast is Gandhā, red in color, holding a scent-conch and a sword in her left and right hands respectively. In the east is Ādarśā, white, with two arms holding a mirror. In the south is Rasā, red, with two hands holding a vessel of nectar. In the west is Sparśā, green, with two arms holding various garments. In the north is Dharmā, white, with two arms holding a white *dharmodayā*.

And these deities, Vairocana and the others, have one face and three eyes; they wear crowns of matted hair, are adorned with five skulls, wheels, and so forth, are clad in divine garments, and perform the *tāṇḍava* dance while seated in the half-lotus posture.

At the eastern gate is Vajrāṅkuśī, sky-blue in color, with faces that are black on the right and white on the left; she has six arms, holding in her right hands a hook, a sword, and a wheel, and in her left hands a noose, a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), and a bell. To the south is Vajrapāśī, white and yellow, with faces that are black on the right and red on the left; she has six arms, bearing in her right hands a noose, a vajra, and a sword, and in her left hands a wheel, a bell, and a noose accompanied by a threatening gesture.

In the west is Vajrasphoṭā, red in color, with faces that are black and white on the right and left respectively, and six arms; her right hands hold a chain, a vajra, and a sword, while her left hands hold a wheel, a bell, and a goad. In the north is Vajraghaṇṭā, green in color, with faces that are black and white on the right and left respectively, and six arms; she holds a bell, a vajra, and a sword in her right hands, and a wheel, a goad, and a noose in her left hands.

These four [deities] have three eyes on each face; their tawny hair is crowned with flames; they are adorned with ornaments such as garlands of five skulls; they wear garments of tiger-skin and dance in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon a sun-disk within a skull-cup on a universal lotus. Ratnasaṃbhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi are situated upon a sun-disk within a skull-cup on a universal lotus. All other deities, however, are situated upon a moon-disk within a skull-cup on a universal lotus. Yet all of them possess the radiance of the sun.

Having thus arranged this mandala of deities consisting of thirty-seven [deities], one should expand the hook of light rays from the heart; then, having urged forth Vajrāṅkuśī through the internal light rays of the heart, while pronouncing the syllable *jaḥ*, one should summon the maṇḍala of gnosis (*jñānamaṇḍala*) by means of the wrathful deities emitted from the heart. Having brought it before oneself and established it there, one should offer water for the face and water for the feet, and worship it. Then, by means of Vajrapāśī—who has been urged forth by the light rays of the heart—while pronouncing the syllable *hūṃ*, the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*) is raised up by the white light rays emitted from the heart.

Reciting “Oṃ kuru kuru samayādhipati hūṃ jaḥ svāhā,” one should invoke [the deity] and cause him to enter one’s own wheel (*svacakra*) preceded by the *kamalāvarta* gesture. Likewise, while uttering the syllable *baṃ*, one should perform the binding by means of yellow rays of light issuing from the heart through the *vajrasphoṭa* gesture, which pervade the mandala. Similarly, while uttering the syllable *hoḥ* with the *vajraghaṇṭā*, one should effect satisfaction by means of red rays of light that cover the mandala. In all cases, one should accomplish the empowerment of the eyes and so forth, the empowerment of body, speech, and mind, and the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*) through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).

By the rays from the seed-syllable in the heart of the Lord of the Maṇḍala, the Tathāgatas are exhorted, as are the five Yoginīs who have been pleased by him. With jeweled vases filled with the water of the five wisdoms, they simultaneously bestow the empowerment upon all [the deities] as before; one should visualize the manifestation of the Family Lord (*kuleśa*) upon the crown. In that regard, for the Tathāgatas beginning with Vajrasattva—namely Māmakī, Śabdavajrā, Gītā, Sparśavajrā, and Dharmadhātuvajrā—the Family Lord is Akṣobhya.

Vairocana is the lord of Locanā, Vajraraudrī, Pṛthivīvajrā, Puṣpā, Hāsyā, Vaṃśā, and Vajrāṅkuśī; Ratnasaṃbhava is the lord of Vajraḍākinī, Vajrabimbā, Dhūpā, Lāsyā, Vīṇā, and Vajrapāśī; Amitābha is the lord of Pāṇḍarā, Vajrarāgī, Dīpā, Gandhā, Mukundā, and Vajrasphoṭā; and Amoghasiddhi is the lord of Tārā, Vajrasaumyā, Vajrayakṣī, Nṛtyā, Rasā, Murajā, and Vajraghaṇṭā.

Then, one should cause the host of goddesses—who have been drawn in by the rays of light from the seed-syllables of the sixteen goddesses situated within the interior of the lotus, which contains the liquid *bodhicitta* consisting of the Tathāgatas drawn in by the seed-syllable at the heart and entered through the mouth—to enter through the mouth of the [central] goddess and fall right there in the form of liquid *bodhicitta*.

Then, from the rays of the bodhicitta with seed-syllables issuing forth from the pores of wisdom (*prajñā-romakūpa*), one should emit a host of goddesses and various offerings of worship, and worship the maṇḍala with the mantra: *oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjāvajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*. Then, with the eight-line mantras to be recited in the thirty-second [chapter], one should praise the Blessed One through the faces of the goddesses. Furthermore, one should resolve upon him being saluted, praised, and entreated by all sentient beings impelled by those rays of light.

Then, having prepared the nectar according to the procedure to be described in the thirty-fourth [chapter], one should—through the impulsion of light rays from the heart—mentally draw it into each of the thirty-seven vessels, or into that which is held in the hand, by means of the tubes of light from the tongue that is a white *hūṃ* syllable and a single-pronged vajra; thus, one should taste it without attachment. One should also examine the reality of the mandala both conventionally (*saṃvṛti*) and ultimately (*paramārtha*). This is the second meditative absorption (*samādhi*), named "The Supreme King of Mandalas."

Thereafter, all the deities of the maṇḍala, impelled by the Vajra-holder, as well as the Blessed One, having produced for others the capacity for their welfare and the attainment of the state of the Great Vajra-holder through the pervasive emanations of their bodily arrays that fill the expanse of the sky, should reabsorb those bodily arrays into their own fundamental bodies; this is the third meditative stabilization, named "The Supreme King of Ritual Actions."

Thereafter, desiring to stabilize the mind for the swift accomplishment of all siddhis, one should meditate on the syllable *aṃ* located at the navel, heart, throat, and great bliss wheel (*mahāsukhacakra*) within the hollows of the knots. This *aṃ* is of the nature of Caṇḍālī, impelled by the wind and fire residing in the secret wheel. One should visualize this *aṃ* as being melted by its blazing rays and becoming inseparable from the three syllables beginning with *haṃ*, thus transforming into a drop (*bindu*) consisting of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). Having gained conviction through the maturation of this meditation, [one should then draw forth] from that very [drop] a subtle...

One should visualize a line of light rays remaining like a single blazing flame. By its power, the drop (bindu), flooded by a flowing torrent of nectar, and that line of light rays, shall become cooled. Then, with the mind fixed upon the drop, one should gaze at it until stability is regained, as indicated by the signs (nimitta).

Once stability has been observed, one should clearly contemplate the light of that line of rays illuminating the entire universe; then, one will see everything like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand and swiftly accomplish all meditative absorptions—this is the *binduyoga*.

Alternatively, once the world has been transformed into a perfect Buddha by the Tathāgatas emerging from the mass of light rays of the heart-mantra, one should fix the mind upon the syllable *hūṃ* in the form of a drop (*bindu*) within that [world], for as long as desired. Then, through the process of exhalation, having illuminated everything up to the vajras of body, speech, and mind with those light rays, one should resolve that the mandala—suddenly manifested within the seed-drop—is withdrawn in the form of inhalation.

Furthermore, having again illuminated the world by the radiation of rays in the form of exhalation, and having resolved upon the benefit for the world being performed by the Tathāgatas who have issued forth from those rays, one should illuminate one’s own heart in the form of inhalation; one may do this as long as desired—this is another *binduyoga*.

Alternatively, one should contemplate that the *bodhicitta*, melted by the rays of the Samādhisattva, travels via the *avadhūtī* to the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), and returning by that same path, abides in the form of a subtle atom through identity with the *hūṃ-bindu* at the heart; such is the *binduyoga*.

Following that, since the cultivation of subtle yoga (*sūkṣmayoga*) is the supreme means for stabilizing the mind, one should visualize as follows: having established at the tip of the *vajra*—or at the tip of the nose of the lotus—the drop of bodhicitta consisting of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), which is of the single flavor of the melted syllable *Aṃ* and so forth, the size of a mustard seed, instantly perfected and accompanied by the maṇḍala; and once it has descended from there, one should observe it. Having seen the signs of stability as described, one should emanate the maṇḍala; this is subtle yoga.

Alternatively, one should meditate on a vajra or similar object, the size of a mustard seed, which has been instantly manifested and accompanied by a maṇḍala; this object is produced from the seed-syllable generated by the melting of the Tathāgatas who have entered through the mouth, drawn in by the rays of light from the heart-mantra. Having placed it at the tip of the lotus at the end of the nose with the tip of the vajra, one should meditate upon it. Or, as before, one should emanate [the deities] or contemplate the subtle yoga according to one's preference.

Thereafter, the white syllable *oṃ*, having emanated the Buddhas and others, enters together with the wind and remains upon the short white form situated within the heart-lotus; then, while establishing those emanations in a continuous flow together with the wind, the red syllable *āḥ* emerges together with the wind and withdraws the emanations; finally, the black syllable *hūṃ* should be meditated upon. As it has been said: "By means of entry, abiding, emergence, and following, through the recitation that follows the meaning—which is without intrinsic nature and beautiful. (*Pañcakrama* 1.25ab, 1.43cd)

"One should recite the mantra with its limbs unseparated, abiding in the state of wisdom and means. For this very reason, because it is of a non-dual nature, this is not a recitation by a neuter. [Objection: But how can Buddhahood arise from speech and conceptual construction? [Reply: True; however, through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddha, all that is accomplished effortlessly (*anābhoga*).

Thus, having brought this into manifestation through the yoga of the great maṇḍala, *vajrajāpa*—which consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*) and bestows the great accomplishment—is said to be that which effects the welfare of the world by means of the recitation of mantras that illuminate the reality (*tattva*) of the body and so forth, and by way of various limitless emanations and reabsorptions adorned with manifold offerings and oblations.

Within this very context, other types of recitation are established as follows: the mere utterance of the mantra is *mantrajāpa*; the mere recollection of the deity-yoga is *rūpajāpa*; and the contemplation of the mere reality is *yoga*. Furthermore, *mantrajāpa* is of many kinds.

In that regard, reciting either the heart-mantra or the near-heart-mantra from the seed-syllable at the heart, one should emanate the host of deities of the mandala, cause them to accomplish the welfare of the world, and then—by means of the mantra itself, according to the analogy of drawing in a thread with a bead—cause them to enter back into that very seed-syllable at the heart by means of the wind. At the conclusion of the recitation of each individual deity-mantra, there is an emanation and reabsorption for each; this is the *samaya*-recitation (*samayajapa*).

With the sense of the equality of all phenomena (*sarvadharmasamatāhaṃkāra*), one should recite the *mālāmantra* while visualizing it as follows: having entered one's own mouth, it proceeds through the path of the *vajra*, goes to the *padma*, rises up by way of the *avadhūtī*, issues from the mouth of the Blessed Lady, enters the gateway of one's own mouth, and thus revolves. This is the "pendulum recitation" (*dolājāpa*) consisting of relaxed and peaceful syllables. This very same practice, distinguished merely by its entry into the mouth of the Blessed Lady and its exit from one's own mouth, is the "fierce recitation" (*krūrajapa*) consisting of dense and harsh syllables.

The recitation of the heart-mantra and so forth constitutes the wrathful recitation (*krodhajapa*). In that regard, the heart-mantra of Vajrasattva is: *oṃ vajrāmṛta mahāsukha hūṃ svāhā*. The near-heart-mantra (*upahṛdaya*) is: *oṃ āḥ hūṃ hūṃ svāhā*.

Oṃ! Homage to the Blessed One, the Lord of Heroes, who resembles the fire at the end of a great aeon; whose crown of matted hair is formidable; whose face is terrifying with fierce, gaping fangs; who is radiant with a thousand arms; who wields an axe, a noose, a raised trident, and a *khaṭvāṅga*; who is clothed in a tiger skin; whose body is like a great smoky darkness. Kara kara! Kuru kuru! Bandha bandha! Trāsaya trāsaya! Kṣobhaya kṣobhaya! Hrauṃ hrauṃ hraḥ hraḥ pheṃ pheṃ phaṭ phaṭ! Burn, burn! Cook, cook!

"Eat, eat! O you who hang garlands of fat, blood, and entrails! Seize, seize! Whether it be a serpent or a snake dwelling in the seven netherworlds, threaten, threaten! Drag, drag! Hrīḥ hrīḥ jñauṃ jñauṃ kṣmāṃ kṣmāṃ hāṃ hāṃ hīṃ hīṃ hūṃ hūṃ kili kili sili sili hili hili dhili dhili hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā! This is the *mālā-mantra*. As for the Blessed Lady’s [root mantra]: "Oṃ vajravairocanīye buddhaḍākinīye svāhā! This is the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*).

As he will say: "This sixteen-syllable mantra is the root mantra of Ḍākinī. This is also called the heart mantra in some places. *Oṃ vajravairocanīye* is the near-heart mantra. These maṇḍala deities' mantras are also to be recited; all of them will be explained. As for the Bhagavatī’s garland mantra:

Oṃ! Homage to the Blessed Lady Vajravārāhī, the Noble Invincible One, Mother of the Three Worlds, Sovereign of Great Knowledge, who brings fear to all beings; O Great Vajra, seated upon the vajra-throne, unconquered, invincible, the one who brings others under control, the whirler, the dryer of poison, the wrathful, the furious, the terrifying, the slayer, the excellent piercer, the conqueror, the victorious, the crusher, the subduer, the deluder—O Vajravārāhī, Great Yoginī, Mistress of Desire, O Sky-goer! It is as follows: *protaṅge protaṅge*, strike, strike!

O Kiṅkiṇi, Khiṅkhiṇi, shake, shake the life-breaths! O Vajrahastā, dry up, dry up! O bearer of the vajra, skull-cup, and khaṭvāṅga; O devourer of great flesh and meat; O you clothed in human entrails; O wearer of a garland of human heads strung together; O Sumbhani, Sumbhe! Strike, strike the life-breaths of all sinful beings and of all sacrificial animals! O cutter of the flesh! O embodiment of wrath! O you with terrifying fangs! O Mahāmudrā, chief queen of the glorious god Heruka, thousand-headed, thousand-armed!

O you with a hundred thousand faces, blazing with splendor! O Jvālāmukhī, with tawny eyes, whose body is of vajra and whose seat is of vajra! Mili mili, timili timili! He he, ha ha, hūṃ hūṃ, kha kha! Budhu dhuru dhuru, muru muru! O non-dual Great Yoginī, perfected by recitation! Dreṃ dhaṃ dreṃ dhaṃ, graṃ graṃ! He he, ha ha! O Terrible One, laugh, laugh! O Heroine, hā hā, hoḥ hoḥ, hūṃ hūṃ! O Destroyer of the three worlds, surrounded by a retinue of thousands of millions of Tathāgatas! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! O you in the form of a lion!

Khaḥ! O you in the form of an elephant, Gaḥ Āḥ! O you who contain the three worlds within your belly, whose girdle is the ocean, swallow, swallow! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! In the non-duality of heroes, hūṃ hāḥ hāḥ! O deluder of great beasts, O Great Yoginī, you are the Ḍākinī, the one praised by all the worlds, the one who produces immediate conviction, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ! O terrifier of spirits, O Great Heroine, O Supreme Siddha-Yoginī, phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!

Exhausted by meditation and recitation, one should visualize the semen (*śukra*) of the *mahāsukha-cakra*—melted by the rays from the heart-seed syllable and drawn in by those Tathāgatas with whom it has become unified—as a rain of streams of semen consisting of great bliss, pervading the entire body; having thus performed the nourishment (*āpyāyana*), one should rest for a moment and then meditate and recite as before.

Desiring to dismiss [the deities], one should offer the *bali* according to the sequence to be described, perform the worship and other rites as before, dissolve the maṇḍala into the heart-mantra consisting of the three syllables, and make aspiration prayers (*praṇidhāna*). Then, having risen with a purified mind, visualizing the Blessed One’s form embraced by the Blessed Lady, and resolving that oneself and the limitless triple world are illusory in nature and of the essence of great bliss whose sole flavor is emptiness, one should accomplish the worship for one's own happiness and the welfare of others through conduct as one pleases.

At the time of bathing, one should perform the ritual of consecration (*abhiṣeka*). Satisfying the syllable *HŪṂ* according to the ritual for tasting nectar (*amṛtāsvāda*), one should partake [of the food].

In the event of a transgression of the commitments (*samaya*), one whose heart is adorned with the wheel of Amoghasiddhi and the crossed double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) should, as prescribed, meditate on the world as naturally pure and consecrate oneself as before. However, in the case of faults such as disrespecting the guru, one should feed the gurus according to one's ability, give gifts, ask for forgiveness, and take up the vows once more; thus one should perform the restoration of the commitments (*samayotthāpana*).

In the intervals between the junctions (*saṃdhyā*), one should emanate the mandala-circle from the heart-seeds and perform the worship and other rites as before. At the conclusion of all junctions, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra that will be described below. One who wishes to lie down should realize that all verbal activity consists of the vowels and consonants (*āli-kāli*):
Oṃ, come, come, O Great Hero, teacher of the pure word;
you who arise from emptiness and wisdom, and from the process of emanation and withdrawal.

Having uttered the syllables from *a* to *kṣa*, followed by *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, one should resolve that oneself consists of the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) whose nature is emptiness, and that sleep has the nature of clear light (*prabhāsvara*). Thus, being of the nature of wisdom and method, one should sleep. Again, at the morning twilight, having arisen from the clear light and recited everything beginning with *oṃ ehy ehi*, the beginner should perform the entire ritual exactly as before without omission. However, if distracted, one should follow the procedure for the other twilights.

However, at the appropriate time, one should accomplish everything. He who obtains the aforementioned signs, being firm-minded in the initial yoga and having gained some mastery over knowledge, should diligently and swiftly construct the mandala and perform the meditation. Furthermore, he whose mind is steady upon the entire mandala through practice has attained mastery over knowledge; manifesting the welfare of the world through emanation and reabsorption, and by realizing the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), he brings the bodhicitta to manifestation and removes even the most subtle of impurities.

Then, through the excellence of cultivation, having attained the siddhi of Mahāmudrā according to the ritual procedure, one becomes master of correct knowledge and capable of accomplishing the welfare of others without limit. However, when the cultivation of the dharmas of laughter, play, song, dance, looking in a mirror, tastes, and touch is not performed, then this very procedure for the cultivation and so forth of the maṇḍala consisting of thirty deities does not apply.

But when, having set aside those eight, the great bodhisattvas such as Maitreya and others are visualized on the panels in the third enclosure, then this very same procedure for visualization and so forth applies. Therein, on the eastern panel are Maitreya and Kṣitigarbha; on the southern, Vajrapāṇi and Khagarbha; on the western, Lokeśvara and Mañjuśrī; and on the northern, Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin and Samantabhadra.

Mañjuśrī is born from the syllable *maṃ*, is reddish-brown like saffron, bears a crown of matted hair sealed by Akṣobhya, has three eyes, and five mudrās. He holds a vajra and a vajra-bell in his two hands, has one face, and stands in the *ālīḍha* posture. Maitreya is born from the syllable *maiṃ*, is golden in color, bears a crown of matted hair sealed by Vairocana, has three eyes, and five mudrās. He holds a *nāgakeśara* flower and a vajra-bell in his two hands, has one face, and stands in the *ālīḍha* posture. The other six [deities] are as described in the section on the empowerment of the eye and so forth.

In this view, however, Maitreya presides over the head; Mañjuśrī presides over all the sensory cognitions (*indriyajñāna*). Regarding the three positions, one view is that the Blessed One Vajrasattva alone is embraced by the aforementioned Prajñā, while all other deities are without Prajñā. A second view is that they are accompanied by their own respective Prajñās. In the ritual for all activities (*sārvakarmika*), Vajravārāhī and Vajrasattva have the colors as previously described: white in pacification (*śāntika*), yellow in enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), and red in subjugation (*vaśya*).
"The two Kṛṣṇas are to be understood as cruel"— here, another systematic arrangement is also to be understood, as stated in the *Yamāritantra*:
"The generation of Vajrasattva is designated as 'yoga'."
For that which is proclaimed as the *anuyoga* is the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of that;
the accomplishment (*niṣpatti*) of the entire wheel is manifested as the *atiyoga*.
It is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the divine eye and so forth, as well as of body, speech, and mind.
"The entry into the wheel of gnosis, the tasting of nectar,
the great worship, the praise, and also the great yoga— these are intended. Furthermore, here in the *Śrīsamāja*:

“O Blessed Ones, all Tathāgatas, headed by Akṣobhya, [you] display the drama of performing deeds for the benefit of sentient beings through many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of vidyās throughout all world-systems, extending to the limits of the world-systems in the ten directions; you sport, delight, and take pleasure with the five strands of sensual desire, yet you do not look upon those devoted to the practice of mantra,” and so forth.

From this instruction, they teach the procedure for accomplishing the *haṭha* [forceful] method. Even at the end, having practiced the vow of the vidyā for as long as six months, with the wrathful deities radiated from the light rays of the heart and oneself with palms joined in reverence, one should supplicate the Buddhas in the ten directions for the sake of accomplishing the *siddhi*. Then, being either authorized or unobstructed in meditative absorption or in a dream, for the purpose of enjoying the offerings and gifts and for the purpose of bestowing the *siddhi*, one should likewise invite them in the evening and manifest the *sādhana*-maṇḍala.

It should be practiced in that very manner. Nevertheless, if [the deity] is still not perceived, one should mentally take refuge in the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, worship them, and ask for their forgiveness; then, the six-month-long vow of the vidyā should be performed once more. Thereafter, it should be practiced in the same way. If [the deity] is still not perceived, one should again perform the six-month-long vow of the vidyā in that same manner and act accordingly. Even if there is still no success, this faultless yogin should employ forceful means (*haṭhasādhana*).

Through the union of one’s own two-fold wisdom (*vidyā*), by means of the yoga of Vairocana as the black, wrathful *samāṇḍaleya*, one should summon Vairocana with the light from the seed-syllable in the heart. Having placed him—extremely terrified and trembling—within the lotus of the consort upon the fire-mandala of Caṇḍālī in his manifested form, one should produce Yamāntaka-Kīlaka, whose nature is bodhicitta, emerging from the path of the vajra after the host of Tathāgatas has been drawn in by the hook of the heart-rays, entered through the mouth, and melted by the yoga of wisdom (*prajñā*). In that same manner, [one produces] the black Vairocana.

One should produce another [deity]. Then, having brought forth Vairocana and pressed him with one's own secret vajra, one should perform the ritual of staking with pride while reciting: "Oṃ āḥ chinda chinda hana hana daha daha! O blazing wheel, Vairocana-vajra, or the deity of the Vairocana family, stake him! Hūṃ phaṭ! while holding the neck of the stake with the left and right hands and striking with a mallet.

Then, immediately after the stake has been driven in, whether the deity is actually present before one or not, and even if not specifically visualized, having stood within one's own maṇḍala, one should drive [the stake] out with the mantra: *oṃ āḥ vajrakīla utkīlaya hūṃ*. Then, while reciting *oṃ ruru sphura jvala tiṣṭha siddha locane svāhā*, one should consecrate [the site] with eyes radiating light from the heart-flame, and perform worship, praise, the tasting of nectar (*amṛtāsvāda*), and the request for forgiveness (*kṣamaṇa*).

One should practice in this manner for up to seven days, and success (*siddhi*) will occur. This is the forceful practice (*haṭhasādhana*) of Vairocana and the deities of his family. Likewise, through the yoga of Kṛṣṇakruddhāmitābha and the stake (*kīlaka*) of Raktapadmāntaka, with the mantra *oṃ āḥ hrīḥ bhūr bhuvaḥ amitābhakula ... laya hūṃ phaṭ*, there is specifically the forceful practice of Amitābha and those belonging to his family.

Likewise, through the yoga of Kṛṣṇa, Akṣobhya, Ratnasaṃbhava, and Amoghasiddhi, with a stake [inscribed] with "Oṃ Āḥ Vajrarāja! Nail down Akṣobhya, Ratnasaṃbhava, Amoghasiddhi, or the deity of that family—Hūṃ Phaṭ! one should nail them down. This is the specific method for the accomplishment of Akṣobhya and the others. All of this brings about success only when performed by one who is firmly intent upon the nailing, the stake, and the act of nailing.

In that case, are the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, dependent on others, such that compassionate yogis must accomplish [their aims] by force against those who do not bow? Has it not been stated in the *Samāja*—
the *Guhyasamājatantra* (10.13d)— that "this arises from drama"?

This drama of the Buddhas is, for some reason, merely a play performed by yogins who do not perceive any other excellence in the minds of yogins, and by those yogins themselves, like an actor, for the sake of pleasing the Tathāgatas. And those Blessed Ones, as if terrified—though they are not actually terrified—perform yet another drama out of being overcome by compassion. As it is said in the *Guhyasamājatantra* (10.15):
"The givers of boons look on, terrified, their minds trembling."

"They bestow vast accomplishment, which is dear to the satisfaction of the mind. Thus he speaks of the maṇḍala of the two-armed Heruka, who delights in the cremation ground. "On the outside," and so forth. "As before" means like the maṇḍala of Vajrasattva, endowed with squareness and other features, and accompanied by the twenty-eight deities beginning with Vajraraudrī. Within that outer maṇḍala, at half its size, is an inner maṇḍala in the shape of a half-moon. "Outside" refers to the four lines beyond the three lines of the garland of vajra-rays; there are the rows of lotuses and wheels, and within them reside all the deities, beginning with Vajrasattva.

He states the distinction: "Gaurī and the others. This refers to the locations of the eight [deities] beginning with Vairocana. In the center, at the place of Vajrasattva, is the seed-syllable for the arising of Heruka; for Gaurī and the others, the seed-syllables are *hīḥ*, *hrīḥ*, and so forth. Furthermore, their names, placements, colors, hand-symbols (*cihna*), and so on, are as described in the sixteen-armed maṇḍala. Regarding the phrase "in the outer maṇḍala," this is because of its semicircular shape.

Regarding the phrase "as before," some masters say that in order to dispel the doubt that this refers to the sixteen-armed mandala, and to indicate the seed-syllables (*bīja*) for the deities of the Vajrasattva mandala as appropriate according to the mantras to be recited later, he states the seed-syllables *oṃ* and so forth for Vaṃśā and the others. Other masters describe this as a two-layered mandala consisting of seventeen deities: the Blessed One and Gaurī and the others in the central layer, and Vaṃśā and the others in the second layer.

The *Vajramarīcimālā* consists of the deity-lineage and the cloth-scrolls. "External" means outside of the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*). *Harivāsa* is the sandalwood tree. The host of gods is Śakra. *Megharāja* is Varuṇa, because of his sovereignty over the clouds. "The army of yakṣas" refers to Kubera, who is thus described as one whose soldiers are yakṣas. Agni is "crowded with a host of sages," because he is surrounded by sages. The *rākṣasa* is Nairṛti.

The *pretas* and the hosts beginning with *Bhṛṅgin* have departed far from the teaching of the Tathāgata; thus, the one to whom their assembly (*saṅgha*) is subject is Śaṅkara, the Lord of the *preta*-assembly. In some cases, there is a non-co-referential (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*) *bahuvrīhi* compound: the hosts together with Rudra, and the gods together with Upendra. [This includes] those headed by Candra, Arka, and Brahmā. Yama is an indicative term for Varuṇa and the others. Who can grasp a portion of these—the mass of sentient beings residing in their respective directions?

He is sealed by those lords of the directions and others—who have not practiced compassion or wisdom, who have habituated themselves to harming others, who are possessed by Māra, or who are created by Vāmāra—and thus rendered powerless in the performance of wholesome deeds, deluded, inverted regarding what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, and devoured by the exhaustion of their side of virtue. "Consisting of ashes" means that even the very ash has been devoured, because even their auspicious latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been destroyed. May the Blessed One restore them to life by overcoming them and performing the opposite of each of those [actions].

(408v/820) This is the synthesis here even according to what is stated in other tantras. To the east of the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) is the cremation ground named Caṇḍogra, which has the alternative name Sādhakānugraha. The tree is *haricandana*. The world-guardian is the elephant-faced Indra, who possesses great supernatural power (*maharddhika*), as is Viṣṇu; the serpent is the white Vāsuki; and the cloud is named Garjita. In the southeast is the cremation ground named Aṭṭahāsa, which has the alternative name Mahāpralaya. The tree is *karañja*. The fire-god is goat-faced and possesses great supernatural power; the serpent is the white Mahāpadma; and the cloud is Ghana.

In the south is the cremation ground named Karaṅkabhīṣaṇa, also known as Ghorāndhakāra; [there dwell] Āmra, Mahiṣamukha, Maharddhika, Yama, Śubhrapadma, Āvarta, and Megha. In the southwest is the cremation ground named Kilikilārava, also known as Mahāmelāpakayogabahula; [there dwell] Parkaṭī, Śavāsya, Maharddhika, Rākṣasa, Nīlānanta, and Prapūraṇa Megha.

In the west is the cremation ground Jvālākula, also known as Krodhānalapara; its tree is Kaṅkelli, its deity is Makaramukha of great supernatural power, its nāga is Varuṇa, its serpent is Harita-karkoṭaka, and its cloud is Ghora-megha. In the northwest is the cremation ground Ghorāndhakāra, also known as Siṃhanāda-mahāphetkāra; its tree is Arjuna, its deity is Mṛgamukha of great supernatural power, its nāga is Vāyu, its serpent is Karburakulika, and its cloud is Varṣaṇa.

In the north is the Gahvara cremation ground; the *aśvattha* tree named Advaitakara; the human-faced Maharddhika; Kubera and Vināyaka with their good armies; the red Takṣaka; and the swirling cloud. In the northeast is the cremation ground named Lakṣmīvana; the *vaṭa* tree named Sarojavīra; the cow-faced Maharddhika; Īśāna; the yellow Śaṅkhapāla; and the fierce cloud. In every case, a *caitya* is to be seen there, upon which [the deity] is mounted on Airāvaṇa, white [in color], and so forth.
Everything up to "with hand occupied by a *ḍamaru* drum" (410r/823) is to be understood here as that which will be described in the thirty-fourth [chapter].
There are eight hooded serpents with human faces who are well-adorned and not further specified;
these sixteen, beginning with Śakra, have their beloveds cradled in their left laps.

Near the trees, one should recognize the fires of the Rākṣasas by their hands being devoid of grace; those of the Sun are in the sun, and the others, possessing the luster of the moon, are in the moon.
Having abandoned the protection of the Lord, these eight of great supernatural power—whose crowns shine with jewels—[proclaimed]: "The Lord wears a jeweled crown. Thus said some.
Some clouds display half their former bodies, with hands offering skull-cups;
others are intent on the gesture of seizing, having given their left [sides] as an offering;
while the clouds in the sky are of every color.
Some [trees] produce flashes of lightning and rain-showers;

these [forests] are further adorned by various excellent trees, made terrible by crows, owls, vultures, dogs, jackals, lions, boars, tigers, and the like, and rendered most wondrous by snakes such as the *gonāsa*. They are fearsome with skeletons, tridents, hanging half-burnt skulls, knees, headless trunks (*kabandha*), bone-fragments, and the like, and are filled on this side with various *siddhas* and *vidyādharas*, groups of *yogins* and *yoginīs* observing their vows, and *yakṣas*, *vetālas*, *rākṣasas*, and others who are shouting "kili-kili."
Then [he saw] great cremation grounds, most wondrous to behold, filled with beings running, moving, standing, sitting, and lying down.

Within the interior of the gabled pavilion surrounded by these [deities], the Blessed Lord Saṃvara is dark blue in color, his hair-tuft crown marked with a jewel, a crossed-vajra, a crescent moon, and Akṣobhya; he wears a garland of skulls above his forehead, possesses the six mudrās, has three eyes and one distorted face, and is adorned with a hanging garland of severed heads. With tiger skin slipping from the front and draped behind, he holds a khaṭvāṅga in the manner of a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and embraces Vajravārāhī—who holds a skull-cup filled with blood—in his left arm.

His right arm raised, wielding a trembling vajra, he performs the *tāṇḍava* dance in the half-lotus posture while treading upon Viśvāmbhoja, Bhānu, Bhairava, and Kālarātri, manifesting the nine sentiments of dramatic art.

And the Blessed Lady should be understood as follows: she is red, three-eyed, with disheveled hair, and a row of skulls bound upon her forehead. She bears the five mudrās, is naked, adorned with a girdle of bone fragments, and wears a hanging garland of dried heads. Her left hand cradles her Lord, holding a skull-cup filled with a continuous stream of blood being drunk by the Blessed One; her right hand brandishes a vajra with the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*). Enveloping his two shanks, she generates great bliss.

He states another alternative: "Furthermore," and so forth. This one is devoid of wisdom (*niṣprajña*), has two arms in the fierce posture (*raudrāsana*), and there is another distinction as before. Regarding the phrase "of Brahmā and the others" (*brahmādīnām*): having stepped upon and overcome Brahmā and the rest, he enjoys the goddesses such as Brahmāṇī; and the connection is that he bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*) upon sentient beings. With arrays of Tathāgatas equal to Vajrasattva, who are shimmering, there are various rays of light in all directions as they occur.

The sequence of meditation for this Lord—who delights in the cremation ground, who has two arms, and who sits upon a fierce seat with two arms—should be understood as previously described according to the appropriate method; however, it is not analyzed here in detail so that the text may not become overly prolix. The two mantras to be recited for these two [forms] will, however, be stated. "Attains accomplishment" means he attains the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā.
The twelfth mañjarī in the *Āmnāyamañjarī*, a commentary on the *Śrīsampuṭa* composed by the scholar Abhayākaragupta.
